Issue Reading note
The Q1 2026 segment recast moved about $2.0bn a year across the reportable-segment line Orthopaedic Instruments moved from MedSurg's Instruments line into a new Ortho Tech line inside Orthopaedics; Neuro Cranial and spine Enabling Technologies moved into Instruments; $518m of goodwill was reallocated. Segment revenue split shifts from 62.3/37.7 on the FY2025 10-K basis to 54.2/45.8 on the restated H1 2026 basis. FY2025 10-K segment totals do not tie to 2026 10-Q segment totals, and no restated FY2023–FY2025 segment operating income exists in any filing.
Segment operating income is far above GAAP operating income FY2025 total segment operating income was $7,492m (29.8% of sales) against consolidated GAAP operating income of $4,889m (19.5%). The $2,603m gap is Corporate and Other $889m, amortization of intangibles $732m, acquisition and integration $335m, structural optimization $191m, impairments $170m, inventory step-up $173m, medical device regulation $38m, recall $58m and legal $17m. Segment margins of 29.9% and 29.8% cannot be set against 19.5%.
Q1 2026 is not a demand signal and Q2 2026's reported gross margin is not a run-rate A cyber incident on 11 March 2026 wiped roughly 40,000 laptops and stopped global manufacturing for almost three weeks; Q1 organic growth was 2.4% and adjusted EPS declined 8.5%. Q2 2026's 68.3% reported gross margin includes 240bps from a $158m reversal of 2025 tariffs ($158m on $6,589m of quarterly net sales) and, year over year, 110bps of lower inventory step-up amortization; the adjusted figures of 66.0% gross and 27.4% operating margin are the comparable ones.
Several material quantities are disclosed nowhere No dollar capital backlog, order book or remaining performance obligation appears in any 10-K or 10-Q, and it is the stated support for a second half that has to grow roughly 11% organically. No units, ASPs or procedure counts exist for any business line. No country-level revenue exists (United States versus International only), so China volume-based procurement cannot be sized. Segment assets stop being disclosed from Q1 2026, removing the last per-segment return-on-capital denominator.

FY2025's GAAP effective tax rate of 28.1%, against 14.3% in 2024, is a one-year artefact of a $718m charge for intra-entity transfers of intellectual property; management guides FY2026 to a 15–16% adjusted rate. And no sell-side research on Stryker exists in the local store, so every statement about "consensus" below rests on Bloomberg estimate data, management's own narrative and the questions analysts asked on the calls, not on any published note.

1. Business description, model and unit economics

Stryker sells surgical capital equipment, per-procedure implants and single-use disposables to hospitals, ambulatory surgery centres and emergency medical services agencies in about 61 countries. FY2025 net sales were $25,116m across two reportable segments, and 75.7% of that came from the United States (10-K FY2025, Note 14). The company discloses only two geographic buckets; Japan is described as the second-largest country outside the United States and is never sized.

The two segments arrive at almost identical operating margins from opposite cost structures. Orthopaedics runs a 72.9% segment gross margin against 33.1% of sales in SG&A, because implants are consigned to hospital shelves and sold by a rep standing in the operating room. MedSurg and Neurotechnology runs a 62.6% segment gross margin against 25.1% SG&A, because a camera platform or a defibrillator is sold once to a capital committee▪ (10-K FY2025, Note 14).

Revenue is recognised on transfer of control at a point in time; under 10% of company sales are recognised as services over time, which puts the whole company-wide over-time service line below $2,512m and places nearly all of it inside this segment (10-K FY2025, Note 2). Revenue is recognised only when Stryker "has received a purchase order and appropriate notification the product has been used or implanted" (10-K FY2025, Note 2). Stryker therefore owns the implant inventory sitting in every hospital's consignment cupboard until a surgeon opens the box, which is why consolidated inventory was $5,310m at YE2025, 21.1% of sales, 67% of it in finished form, and why days inventory outstanding has never dropped below 197 in the decade.▪

On the restated Q1 2026 basis the segment looks different again. H1 2026 revenue of $5,777m splits Trauma and Extremities 36.5%, Knees 23.6%, Ortho Tech 23.6%, Hips 16.3% and Spinal Implants 0.1% (10-Q Q2 2026, Note 2). Inside Ortho Tech, Orthopaedic Instruments was $1,012m of the $1,363m and Mako plus enabling technologies plus bone cement was $351m. Mako plus enabling technologies plus bone cement is therefore about 6% of the restated segment, and Mako-branded revenue alone is less than that. The robot pulls through the 40% of segment revenue that is knees and hips; it is not itself a revenue line of consequence.▪

1.3 What sets price, volume and cost

Price is zero in Orthopaedics and has decayed to zero in MedSurg. Stryker discloses the price contribution to organic growth every year, and three separate disclosures agree for Orthopaedics: the revenue bridge attributes −0.1% to lower prices in FY2025 and 0.0% in FY2024, H1 2026 and Q2 2026, and the segment operating-margin bridge attributes 0bps to sales pricing in all four periods (10-K FY2025, Item 7; 10-Q Q2 2026, Item 2). MedSurg was the only source of positive price in the group and it is gone: the contribution ran +1.7% (FY2023), +1.7% (FY2024), +0.7% (FY2025), +0.3% (H1 2026) and +0.1% (Q2 2026), and the Q2 2026 segment margin bridge has no sales-pricing line at all.▪ Consolidated price was 0.0% in Q2 2026, the first quarter in three years with none. Zimmer Biomet reports the same picture from the other side: "Global selling prices had a minimal effect on year-over-year sales growth in 2025. The majority of countries in which we operate continue to experience pricing pressure" (ZBH 10-K FY2025, Item 7).

Volume is set by procedure counts and by capital budgets, and the two have different cycles. The implant half tracks elective and non-elective surgical volume. The capital half tracks hospital operating cash flow with a one-to-two-year lag, plus healthcare construction. Neither is disclosed by Stryker, so both are traced through third parties in the driver tree below.

Cost is largely fixed at the plant and variable in the field. MedSurg's incremental dollar produced roughly 74 cents of gross profit over FY2022–FY2025 and re-spent about 29 cents on selling and 6 cents on engineering, for a 38.7% cumulative incremental operating margin (10-K FY2024 and FY2025, Note 14). Orthopaedics' realised incremental margin clusters at 38–44% in normal years against a 73% gross margin, so roughly 30 points of every incremental gross-margin dollar is consumed by the salesforce and R&D needed to produce it.

The highest-margin business inside Stryker is one that has never had a disclosed P&L. Two 10-Qs report the same six-month period on the two bases, which prices the transferred bundle. H1 2025 Orthopaedics was $4,606m of revenue and $1,319m of segment operating income on the old basis, and $5,527m and $1,754m restated (10-Q 2025-Q2 and 10-Q 2026-Q2, segment notes). The $921m of transferred revenue therefore came with $435m of operating income, a 47.2% segment operating margin, on a 64.4% gross margin and 8.6% of revenue in SG&A.▪ The Q2 2025 quarter alone gives 47.6%. Orthopaedic Instruments — power tools and their per-case disposables, which attach to every case regardless of implant vendor and need no per-case rep — is the most profitable disclosed unit in the company, and its economics are visible only by differencing two filings.

That arithmetic is what stands behind management's own warning that "we generally expect segment mix to have an unfavorable impact for the foreseeable future as we anticipate more rapid sales growth in our lower gross margin MedSurg and Neurotechnology segment" (10-K FY2025, Item 7).

The Ventura order matters more than its size because it is the only place Stryker's MedSurg unit economics appear in a primary document. It shows a console at $48,337 on an 8–10 year replacement cycle, attached hardware adding 16.8% at the point of sale, prepaid service at 4.1% of console price a year, a data subscription on top, and a trade-in credit that makes the incumbent's replacement cheaper than a competitor's new install.▪ Over a ten-year life ProCare alone is 41% of the console price. That is a strong annuity on an installed fleet; it is not a subscription business.

1.5 Demand-driver tree

D1 — Elective large-joint procedure count (Knees plus Hips, ~40% of Orthopaedics revenue, 45.2% of FY2022–25 ex-spine growth). Management's word is "the orthopaedic market… mid-single-digit growing" (Q4 2025 call). One level down, Smith+Nephew sizes global Hip and Knee Implants at $17.6bn growing 5% in 2025 (SNN 20-F FY2025). Since price is zero, that 5% is essentially all volume. One level further down, the exposure is the number of patients with end-stage hip or knee osteoarthritis converted to surgery: the 60–85 population, the surgical conversion rate at a given symptom severity, and operating-room capacity. The moving part is site-of-care economics, measurable outside Stryker: Surgery Partners' orthopaedics and pain-management case mix rose from 36.1% of cases in 2023 to 40.7% in 2025, and it estimates annual procedure volume growing about 2% in hospital outpatient departments and about 6% in ambulatory surgery centres while inpatient declines about 2% (SGRY 10-K FY2025). Robustness: structurally growing but deferrable, and the downside amplitude is measurable — in 2020 Knees declined 13.7% and Hips 12.8%, and the Orthopaedics and Spine segment posted a 123% decremental margin. Realised check: confirmed but decelerating, FY2025 Knees +8.2% and Hips +8.9% in constant currency against Q2 2026 Knees +6.2% and Hips +4.9% in the United States.

D2 — Trauma and Extremities case count (36.5% of restated Orthopaedics revenue, 46.4% of FY2022–25 ex-spine growth). This is a different exposure and the tree must not collapse the two. Trauma plating and nailing volume reduces to fragility-fracture incidence, which is non-elective, not deferrable and unresponsive to ASC economics. Extremities reduces to penetration of arthroplasty into joints that were previously not replaced. Smith+Nephew sizes the market at $15.7bn growing 7%. Robustness: the most robust branch in the tree, and 2020 is the decisive test: Trauma and Extremities grew 4.9% in the year Knees declined 13.7%. Realised check: confirmed and holding, FY2025 +11.8% constant currency and Q2 2026 +11.5%, with US +12.5%.

D3 — Share of those procedures, through the Mako channel. Management's framing is "Mako drives share". One level down, the exposure is surgeon switching cost, measurable as the share of a surgeon's caseload already on a Stryker robot: over two-thirds of US knees and over one-third of US hips exiting 2025, roughly 50% and over 20% globally (Q4 2025 call). A level below that, the durability depends on whether the robot is owned, financed or rented, and every ASC Mako is financed (Q4 2023 call), so the fastest-growing channel has the weakest lock. Realised check: share is demonstrated — Stryker gained roughly 100bps of four-player hip-and-knee share and 110bps of Trauma and Extremities share in 2025 — but line growth is not, because the two Mako-exposed lines compounded 90bps a year slower than the ex-spine segment over FY2022–25 and are the two slowest lines in H1 2026.

D4 — Realized price per construct. Ultimately the tender and contracting regime: US hospital and GPO contracting, CMS procedure economics, European national tenders, Japanese biennial reimbursement cuts, and China's volume-based procurement, which the 10-K names explicitly as a mechanism "designed to decrease prices for medical devices". Contribution: zero. Over FY2023–FY2025 Orthopaedics added $1,134m of revenue of which approximately −$9m is price. Management lists pricing discipline as a margin lever on Investor Day slide 66; the segment bridge has shown 0bps for four consecutive reporting periods. This is a hypothesis, not a driver.

D5 — US hospital capital budgets (Instruments, Endoscopy and the capital half of Medical, roughly 55–60% of MedSurg revenue and about 55% of its FY2023–25 organic growth). Not "hospital CapEx budgets remain healthy" and not demographics. Hospital capital spending is funded out of hospital operating cash flow, so the exposure is the US hospital operating margin with a one-to-two-year lag, plus healthcare construction put-in-place for the OR-infrastructure revenue Endoscopy named as its top Q2 2026 US growth driver.▪ Robustness: cyclical and currently at a good point that is starting to turn. Kaufman Hall reports the national adjusted year-to-date hospital operating margin closed 2025 at 1.3%, and through May 2026 national hospital operating margins were down 5% year over year, with the West down 12% and the Midwest and Great Plains down 7% each (kaufmanhall.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web]. Realised check: confirmed for now. Instruments US organic grew 19.1% in Q4 2025 and 8.4% in Q2 2026; Endoscopy US 11.1% then 10.2%; Medical US 13.6% then 13.1%. The warning is that the funding source turned negative in 2026 while the order book being converted in the second half of 2026 was written in 2025. Stryker's own corroboration is European and capital-specific: "a slower capital environment in Europe during the quarter" (Q4 2025 call). The Q2 2026 reference to "a slight slowdown in Europe" is explicitly about procedures, not capital.

D6 — The ASC channel. Two things get conflated. ASC count determines new-site capital purchases and grew only 1.0%, from 6,504 Medicare-certified centres at Q2 2025 to 6,566 at Q4 2025 (ASC Data via Becker's ASC Review, accessed 2026-07-31) [web, unverified — no retrievable permalink]. Procedure migration into existing ASCs determines disposable and implant pull-through and is a function of CMS site-of-service payment differentials. Stryker's only quantification is per-business: "If you look at our [foot and ankle] business, it's now in the high teens percent, pushing 20% of the procedures now being done in ASCs. And you remember before COVID, it was 5%" (Q2 2026 call). Realised check: the driver is real but the mechanism usually named for it is wrong. At 1% ASC-count growth, new sites cannot be a material capital driver; Stryker's gain is procedure migration into an installed channel plus share capture inside it. Management says the rate limit is construction, not demand.

D7 — Municipal and EMS budgets (LIFEPAK, powered cots, stretchers, inside Medical). Local government general funds, development impact fees and paramedic reserves, with no relationship to hospital economics or procedure volumes. The Ventura purchase was funded $830,079 from a Fire Facility and Equipment Mitigation Fee Trust and $456,500 from paramedic cash reserves [web, same source]. The volume driver is a fleet replacement cycle on an 8–10 year monitor life, currently pulled forward by the LIFEPAK 35 launch replacing a LIFEPAK 15 base installed from roughly 2009. Robustness: a one-time replacement wave, not a secular trend. Every fleet converted is a customer that will not buy another monitor for eight to ten years, and the trade-in ratio of 14 units against 20 purchases makes the finite pool visible.

D8 — Vascular procedure penetration. Three different things inside one reported line: ischemic stroke thrombectomy, which is mature and competitive; hemorrhagic and aneurysm flow diversion, which is a product cycle; and VTE mechanical thrombectomy, currently at 14–19% penetration in pulmonary embolism and deep-vein thrombosis against conservative anticoagulation, gated on the PEERLESS II readout of FlowTriever against anticoagulation alone in over 1,200 patients, expected mid-2027 (Investor Day 2025-11-13; Q2 2026 call). Realised check: three disclosures cut against the driver. FY2025 Vascular grew 50.6% reported but organic growth was roughly 2–5% [estimate: Vascular $1,968m less an Inari contribution of $600–635m derived from the 4.7% acquisition impact on segment growth; gives legacy Vascular of $1,333m–1,368m against $1,307m]. In Q4 2025, before any supply problem, management said "Vascular had U.S. organic sales growth of 4.3%… This performance was offset by competitive pressures in our ischemic business." In Q2 2026 Vascular declined 0.7% reported, 1.8% in constant currency and 6.7% in the United States on a supply failure at a single Inari plant, a drag management put "in the ballpark" of 50–75bps of company organic growth. After removing Inari, Vascular contributed roughly 4% of MedSurg's FY2023–25 organic growth on 13% of its revenue. It is an option on a trial readout, not a demonstrated driver.▪

D9 — Infection prevention and workforce economics (Sage, SmartCare). Not "the nursing shortage". The exposure is CMS reimbursement penalties: the Hospital-Acquired Condition Reduction Program and value-based purchasing withhold payment from hospitals in the worst quartile for infections, falls and pressure injuries, so Sage protocols and ProCuity fall prevention are cost-avoidance purchases priced against a regulatory penalty. That is more durable than a discretionary capital purchase and more exposed to any change in CMS penalty design. Realised check: a hypothesis. Management asserts pull-through and bed-share gains without numbers, the prepaid service book declined $27m in H1 2026, and net additions to contract liabilities ran +$118m (2024), +$46m (2025) and −$27m (H1 2026). If subscriptions were scaling, that balance should be building.

Reconciled to the realised record, the tree shows two things. No single line dominates MedSurg's growth: over FY2023–25 the four largest lines contributed 18–21% each. And the line Stryker markets hardest — Vascular — was the segment's worst organic performer over the same window.

2. Key technologies and technical differentiators

Stryker is not a frontier-technology company. It buys categories and then out-iterates the incumbents inside them, and the thing that is hard to replicate is the combination of a twenty-year installed base of robots that anchors implant choice, an implant-plus-robot ecosystem that is deliberately closed, a sales organisation specialised down to 22 business units, and a generational launch cadence that customers budget around.▪ RD&E was $1,623m in FY2025, 6.5% of net sales and flat with 2024. Cumulative RD&E over FY2016–FY2025 was $11,485m against roughly $22.5bn of acquisition spend, so the technology base is bought at least twice as heavily as it is invented. Patent stock at 2025-12-31 was about 5,600 US patents and 9,000 patents in other countries (10-K FY2025).

Mako SmartRobotics. A CT-based, haptically constrained robotic arm for joint arthroplasty. The workflow is a pre-operative CT, a patient-specific plan of implant size, position and alignment, intra-operative registration of the anatomy to the plan, and a robotic arm that holds the saw and physically resists movement outside the planned resection envelope. The surgeon still cuts; the robot prevents the cut from leaving the plan. What it replaces is a mechanical cutting jig, and in the more advanced comparison, computer-assisted navigation. What it sells is a repeatable, teachable procedure that de-risks the case for a lower-volume surgeon and for an ambulatory centre.▪

Competitors use different architectures. Zimmer Biomet's ROSA positions a cutting jig through which the surgeon cuts; J&J's VELYS is imageless with intra-operative mapping; Smith+Nephew's CORI is a speed-modulated handheld burr, also imageless (onlinelibrary.wiley.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web]. Mako's CT requirement is a real cost and radiation burden and is the competitors' main line of attack; it is also what makes the pre-operative plan possible, which is what makes revision and complex-primary applications possible.

Scale is the differentiator, and it compounded slowly. The installed base went from roughly 650 systems at YE2018 to about 1,500 at YE2021 and over 3,000 at YE2025 in more than 45 countries, and cumulative procedures passed two million across Total Knee, Total Hip and Partial Knee▪ (Q4 2018 through Q4 2025 calls; 10-K FY2025). By the Q2 2026 call the figure was over 2.5 million across 47 countries. Third-party estimates put ROSA at 1,300-plus systems and CORI at 1,100-plus globally at YE2025, and VELYS had passed 100,000 cumulative knee procedures as of March 2025 (jnj.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web]. The gap is in cumulative use and applications, not in the existence of a robot.

The clinical evidence does not support the claim that Mako produces better patient outcomes than conventional or computer-assisted knee surgery.▪ The best-designed study is RASKAL, a registry-nested, multicentre, blinded 2×2 factorial randomised trial with 303 patients in modified intention-to-treat and 278 completing two-year follow-up. Robotic-assisted against computer-assisted surgery at two years gave a KOOS-12 mean difference of −2.8 (95% CI −6.4 to 0.9, p = 0.137), and the authors conclude that robotic-assisted surgery and functional alignment "were not superior to computer-assisted surgery and mechanical alignment" (boneandjoint.org.uk, accessed 2026-07-31) [web]. A Mako-specific meta-analysis of 22 studies and 3,738 knees found robotic favoured at 3 months to 1 year (SMD 0.46), but 20 of the 22 are cohort studies, heterogeneity is I² 85–98% and publication bias was detected [web, same publisher]. Robots deliver alignment precision that is measurable and outcomes that are not, on the evidence that exists. Adoption is heading toward roughly 70% of US knee replacements by 2030 from about 44% in 2025 [web, pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40529236, accessed 2026-07-31] on workflow, training economics and ASC standardisation rather than on a demonstrated outcome delta. Mako's advantage is commercial and workflow-based, which matters because a commercial advantage can be attacked by a cheaper competitor that matches the workflow.

The substitution threat is imageless handheld robotics at a lower capital step-up, and Stryker has already conceded the segment.▪ Mako RPS exists because "there is a subset of surgeons that are not ready to move all the way to Mako who are only interested in doing total knees" (Q2 2026 call). THINK Surgical's TMINI is implant-agnostic and passed its 1,000th knee replacement in May 2025, having run cases with a third-party implant [web, orthospinenews.com, accessed 2026-07-31]. An implant-agnostic robot is the direct attack on Mako's lock. Zimmer Biomet has stated a roadmap for a semi-autonomous Monogram mBôs platform in early 2027 followed by a fully autonomous platform at the end of 2027 or early 2028▪ (ZBH Q3 2025 call). Mako is surgeon-controlled haptic guidance, a different architecture; Stryker has not publicly addressed autonomy — the 2025 Investor Day transcript contains no occurrence of "autonomous", "Monogram" or "Zimmer".

Stryker's record of shipping its own robotic roadmap on the first date given is poor. Mako Spine was first guided to "around the middle of the year next [2024]" on the Q3 2023 call and reached full US launch in H2 2025. Mako Shoulder was guided to "the end of '24" on the Q4 2023 call and reached full commercial launch around mid-2026. Both were roughly 12–18 months late. Mako 4 (March 2025) and Mako RPS (full US launch 16 July 2026) landed on time.

3D-printed porous titanium and cementless knees. Additive-manufactured porous titanium surfaces let bone grow directly into the implant, removing bone cement from the construct. This is a materials-and-process technology: the pore architecture, the powder, the build parameters and the post-processing are the whole product, and it requires a decade of survivorship data before surgeons use it at scale. Stryker launched the Triathlon cementless knee in 2013 and reports 99% survivorship of the construct at ten years (Investor Day 2025-11-13). Cementless penetration inside Stryker's own US knee book went from about 26% in 2018 to over 40% in 2020 to 47% in 2021 and is still rising. Mako and cementless are mutually reinforcing because cementless implants have a tighter tolerance for resection error. The limit is physiological: "I don't think cementless knees will get to 100 because of bone quality" (Q4 2025 call), and every major competitor now offers 3D-printed cementless options, so the durable asset is the ten-year registry data, which erodes as rivals' datasets mature▪.

1788 4K camera platform and fluorescence imaging. A 4K surgical video platform that images beyond the visible spectrum: infrared laser excitation of indocyanine green shows perfusion in real time, and the platform is cleared to visualize CYTALUX, a targeted fluorescent agent that lights up cancerous tissue. The barrier is cumulative rather than architectural — the 1788 is the 26th generation of Stryker surgical camera over forty years, and the fluorescence capability itself was bought with Novadaq in 2017. Any one generation is incremental; the accumulated optical, sensor, sterilization and integration engineering is not. The substitution risk is not another camera but the agent pipeline: the value of the modality depends on the imaging agents, and Stryker co-markets rather than owns CYTALUX.

System 9 power tools and the launch cadence. The ninth generation of battery surgical power tools, introducing the first wireless charging in the category, which solves recharging batteries that are already sterile. It is not technically hard; it is commercially hard, and management explains the mechanism precisely. A new generation launches every four to five years on a fixed date, technology that misses the date rolls to the next launch, and "they will understand that in 2 years, Stryker is going to have its new version of power tools, so they're setting money aside for that… And we usually get better price because we're bringing so much value with those additional versions" (Crotty, Investor Day 2025-11-13). This is the one franchise where technology demonstrably supports price, and it is the one that moved into Orthopaedics in the Q1 2026 recast.▪

Inari thrombectomy and the vascular portfolio. Purpose-built large-bore mechanical thrombectomy catheters that physically remove clot without thrombolytic drugs. The hard part is not the catheter but the evidence: Inari's stated competitor is conservative therapy, not another device, so expanding the category requires randomised trials against anticoagulation. Ten funded studies are running, four of them randomised. Set against that, a single-plant concentration for an emergent-procedure line produced a 6.7% US decline in Q2 2026 and lost sales management conceded were gone: "those are procedures you don't sell like capital equipment to… those cases are emergent. We did lose business."

SmartHospital, Vocera and care.ai. Four interoperable layers sold as recurring software subscriptions: clinical communication endpoints, a workflow layer that routes alerts, virtual nursing, and ambient room intelligence that writes actions into the electronic health record. The technical content is integration, not invention, and the market is crowded — Artisight, AvaSure, Caregility, Andor Health, Teladoc and others, in a category growing about 24% a year [web, globenewswire.com, accessed 2026-07-31]. Stryker's advantage is distribution and its own device fleet, not the software. Its own customer states the difficulty plainly. Vanderbilt's CIO, on the video Stryker played at its own Investor Day: "what the clinician needs is the information aggregated in a way that makes sense independent of the vendor." Management concedes the platform "needs to provide open architecture, which it does," which gives away the lock-in. Management sizes the whole smart-hospital category at $2bn a year, 8% of FY2025 net sales at 100% share.

Ranking the assets by how hard they are to reproduce puts the Mako installed base and application library first, three-dimensional printing with ten-year survivorship second, the 26-generation camera franchise and the nine-generation power-tool franchise next, and SmartHospital last. What differentiates Stryker other than technology may matter more: 22 business units each with their own general manager, sales force, marketing, R&D and business-development lead; a commission structure set on pricing and discount level so reps are paid to defend price; 460-plus ASC partnerships averaging seven business units per deal; and roughly 60 acquisitions in ten years plugged into specialised sales forces by integration teams that move from deal to deal.▪

One contradiction is unresolved: the filings name a SONOPET 4 launch in late 2026 while the Q2 2026 transcript names "the Sonopet 3 ultrasonic aspirator". The transcript is a machine-produced text with visible errors elsewhere in the same paragraph, so the filing name is the more reliable.

3. Competitive advantages and moat assessment

3.1 Orthopaedics

Stryker's Orthopaedics segment earns returns well above its cost of capital and the gap over every listed competitor is widening on most measures. The advantage is not the kind that lets the business set its own price. It is a distribution-and-workflow position that converts into volume and share, it has to be paid for with continuous reinvestment in the robot and with acquisitions, and it depends on four rivals continuing to execute worse.▪

On the segment measure Stryker disclosed for FY2025, Orthopaedics earned a 29.8% operating margin against 14.9% for Smith+Nephew's directly comparable Orthopaedics segment and roughly 24.6% for Zimmer Biomet's whole company on a like-for-like adjusted basis▪ (10-K FY2025, Note 14; SNN 20-F FY2025 Note 2.2; ZBH 10-K FY2025). Orthopaedics grew organic net sales 9.5% in FY2025 against Zimmer Biomet's roughly 3.9%, Smith+Nephew Orthopaedics' 5.1% underlying and Johnson & Johnson Orthopaedics' 1.1% reported. Since 2020 the segment added $3.5bn of revenue and $1.2bn of operating income on a $551m increase in identifiable assets, and pre-tax return on segment identifiable assets rose from 8.8% in 2020 to 15.1% in 2025, improving in each of the last four years.

Against that, realized price has been flat or negative in each of the last nine years, cumulatively about -12.2% (10-K MD&A, FY2018 through FY2025). Zimmer Biomet's global knee revenue of $3,322m and hip revenue of $2,094m both exceed Stryker's $2,656m and $1,865m, so Stryker is second by revenue in both categories among the four majors even after a decade of Mako.▪ Share gain runs at roughly 75-125bps a year, which compounds but excludes nobody. And in the most recent clean quarter the pull-through claim failed a head-to-head test: Stryker's hips grew 2.8% while Johnson & Johnson's hips, sold without any comparable robot, grew 4.9%▪ (10-Q Q2 2026; JNJ 10-Q Q2 2026).

Management claims: Mako is an installed-base advantage that drives both share and price. The 10-K's own competitive sentence is narrow and unchanged for a decade — "We are one of four leading global competitors for joint replacement and trauma and extremities products and robotics" — and the generic competition section names no segment-specific advantage beyond "our commitment to innovation, quality and service and our reputation". The spoken claims are stronger: "over 2/3 of our Knees and over 1/3 of our Hips were performed on Mako in the U.S." and "surgeons aren't going to be going backwards" (Q4 2025 call).

External sources: Johnson & Johnson announced in October 2025 its intention to separate its Orthopaedics business "with a targeted completion within 18 to 24 months", to shift its MedTech portfolio "toward higher-growth and higher-margin markets"; the business achieved sales of $9.3bn in 2025 (JNJ 10-K FY2025). Smith+Nephew devotes a pillar of its own plan to "Fixing Orthopaedics" and describes it as "our underperforming Orthopaedics business" (SNN 20-F FY2025). Enovis recorded a $645.0m goodwill impairment in 2024 and a further $1,049.8m in 2025, producing a $1,124.2m operating loss on $2,248.0m of sales, and runs SG&A at 47.6% of sales against Stryker Orthopaedics' 33.1% (ENOV 10-K FY2025). That evidence bears on the economics of sub-scale participation in this market as much as on Stryker's execution, though J&J's stated reason is portfolio-level capital allocation rather than a claim that the market is uninvestable, and Enovis's write-downs are specific to its own acquisitions.

Ground-up view: minimum efficient scale is set by the national instrument fleet and rep network, not by the factory. Selling a joint implant requires size-graded implants on consignment plus loaner trays cleaned, tracked and delivered per case, which is why SG&A at 33.1% of segment sales exceeds cost of sales at 27.1%. A challenger funds that before booking a first case. Switching costs are surgeon-level and asymmetric: once a surgeon has done a few hundred cases on Mako, switching means re-learning a technique and re-training the whole operating-room team, borne by the surgeon and hospital rather than by Stryker. But the lock has a ceiling and excludes nobody: the hospital keeps buying implants from three other vendors for its non-Mako surgeons, and only 30-40% of Mako sites have more than one system.▪ Buyer power is regulated on price: reimbursement is a fixed payment for the procedure, so a hospital that adopts a robot gets no incremental payment for it and the robot has to pay for itself in throughput or length of stay. That is the structural reason nine years of implant price erosion happened.

The share half of management's case is confirmed by the filings; the price half is not. What the evidence supports is narrower: Mako has arrested price erosion rather than reversed it. Orthopaedics price declined about 1.95% a year on average over 2017-2022 and about 0.4% a year over 2023-2025, with 0.0% in both quarters of 2026.▪ That 155bps-a-year improvement is worth roughly $450m of FY2025 segment revenue against a continuation of the old trend [estimate: 2017-2022 mean of -1.95%/yr compounded over 2023-2025 as counterfactual, applied to FY2025 segment revenue of $9,469m; range $400-500m depending on whether 2022's -2.9% outlier is in the base], more than the whole 260bps of segment operating-margin expansion over those two years.

This is not a structural advantage of the Visa or Google search kind, where the business prices above inflation without having to defend the position. Stryker Orthopaedics prices at zero after spending on a fourth-generation robot, a handheld robot, four new Mako applications and roughly 60 acquisitions in ten years. Nor is it the absent-advantage case: returns are far above the cost of capital and the margin gap over the weakest listed peer is about 1,500bps. This is a strong but bounded advantage: excess returns today, defensible for now, widening on most measured gaps, and dependent on continuous reinvestment.

Business-model analogues. Intuitive Surgical is the closest structural match: a capital platform placed into the operating room that annuitizes a per-procedure revenue stream and locks the surgeon's technique to the platform. It holds because Mako, like da Vinci, runs only Stryker's own implants, so the installed base is a closed channel. It breaks because da Vinci faces no equivalently funded alternative in soft-tissue surgery while Mako faces ROSA, CORI, VELYS and Excelsius, and because manual arthroplasty remains a clinically accepted, cheaper fallback.▪ Edwards Lifesciences matches the surgeon-preference implant shape, where the advantage is clinical evidence plus physician training rather than patents; it breaks because Edwards has demonstrated real price realization in transcatheter valves and Stryker Orthopaedics has not in nine years. IDEXX matches the instrument-placed-then-consumable-annuity shape at a similar margin level; it breaks because IDEXX's consumable price is set with the customer while Stryker's implant price is set by hospital procurement and, in China, by volume-based procurement.

3.2 MedSurg and Neurotechnology

The MedSurg advantage is real, category by category rather than company-wide, and it earns excess returns today. It is not structural in the sense that would make it safe from a well-funded attacker, and two of the three erosion markers are already visible in the disclosed numbers.▪

What holds up: the segment compounded revenue at 13.4% a year from $8,345m (2020) to $15,647m (2025) while segment operating margin went from 28.9% to 29.9% and segment gross margin rose from 59.9% (2023) to 62.6% (2025)▪. Growth and margin expansion together is not the pattern of a price-taking business. The named competitor list in Item 1 has barely changed in ten years — Instruments faces the same four names in FY2025 as in FY2016, Endoscopy the same six, and only Medical rotated as Hill-Rom became Baxter and Medline and Ferno-Washington were added. No new entrant has displaced Stryker in a decade of disclosure, in a category requiring FDA clearance, a validated supply chain and a hospital-facing direct sales force.

What does not hold up is pricing and returns. Management describes pricing as a durable capability built through contracting and sales-commission design and guided FY2026 to look "pretty similar" to FY2025. The disclosed price contribution went +1.7%, +1.7%, +0.7%, +0.3%, +0.1% across 2023 to Q2 2026 and the Q2 2026 margin bridge has no pricing line. On returns, Stryker's consolidated ROIC at a normalized 21% tax was 11.4% in 2019 and 11.9% in 2025 — flat over six years while revenue grew 69%, against Boston Scientific moving 9.3% to 12.5% and Medtronic 7.6% to 12.2%.▪ The returns premium over the large diversified medtechs has been competed away; it remains wide against Zimmer Biomet (4.6%), CONMED (8.1%), Smith+Nephew (8.3% group adjusted) and Baxter and Enovis, both negative. Segment-level ROIC cannot be computed at all, because "Information about total assets by segment is not disclosed because such information is not regularly provided to, or used by, our CODM" (10-Q Q2 2026).

The razor-and-blade framing is bounded by the disclosures. Under 10% of group sales are recognised as services over time, and Stryker discloses no recurring-revenue percentage, renewal rate, attach rate, backlog dollar or software-subscription figure anywhere.▪ The only retention number management has ever quantified is Vocera: "The stickiness rate on Vocera is like 98%" (Investor Day 2025-11-13). That is one product line inside a $4,204m business inside a $15,647m segment.

Management and the industrial-organisation view agree on the mechanism and disagree on its durability. Management treats it as self-sustaining: "it's totally continually sustainable" (Q4 2025 call). On the industrial-organisation view it is renewed each cycle by RD&E at about 6% of segment sales, by roughly $5bn of acquisitions in 2025 alone, and by continually re-cutting the sales force into narrower specialist teams. Nothing in the structure prevents a rival from selling a competing 4K camera or defibrillator into the same hospital. The external evidence supports that view: Boston Scientific agreed to buy Penumbra on 2026-01-15 for an enterprise value of about $14.5bn (news.bostonscientific.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web], putting a far better-capitalised competitor into Stryker's fastest-growing MedSurg line; Stryker itself named "competitive pressures in our ischemic business" in Q4 2025; and its own supply failures show customers reallocating within a quarter, which is what a low switching cost looks like.

The segment earns durable returns above its cost of capital and holds a defensible position in most of its categories without a structural moat. The gap over Zimmer Biomet, CONMED and Baxter is widening; the gap over Boston Scientific and Medtronic has closed. The most useful forward marker is price: if MedSurg's price contribution stays near zero through 2027 while the segment keeps growing high single digits, the advantage is volume and share rather than pricing power, and it will be more cyclical than management's framing implies.

Business-model analogues. STERIS is closest by shape — capital equipment plus consumables plus service into the same operating room, serial bolt-on acquisitions, a similar five-year revenue CAGR — but runs a 44.2% gross margin against MedSurg's 62.6% and has a large outsourced-sterilization leg with a different cost structure. Danaher is the analogue for the operating model rather than the products: decentralized specialized units, a named continuous-improvement system, serial tuck-ins folded into existing sales forces. It breaks because Danaher's consumables are qualified into a customer's validated process, so switching requires re-validation, while Stryker discloses no attach or renewal metric and under 10% of revenue as over-time services. Intuitive Surgical is the upper bound of the same installed-base logic and the benchmark for what a razor-and-blade annuity produces: 29.3% GAAP operating margin, 19.1% ROIC and a 24.7% free-cash-flow margin in FY2025, on a consumable contractually attached per procedure. Baxter is the counterexample: the same customer and the same hospital-capital roll-up logic, and a -0.7% five-year revenue CAGR, a 30.1% gross margin and negative GAAP operating margin and ROIC. None of the network-economics references applies; there is no two-sided network in MedSurg and nothing in it excludes a competitor.

3.3 The advantage tested three ways

Standalone. Stryker's own ten-year record on a normalized 15% tax basis: ROIC of 17.2% (2016), 12.3% (2019), 8.7% (2020), 11.7% (2023) and 13.0% (2025). Excluding goodwill and intangibles, ROIC stayed in a 30-40% band throughout and was 37.6% in 2025 against 38.9% in 2019. The operating businesses earn very high returns on tangible capital, and the acquired capital dilutes the consolidated figure.▪ Gross margin declined from 66.3% (2016) to 62.8% (2022) and recovered only to 64.0% (2025). Free-cash-flow margin was 17.1% in FY2025 against a decade range of 7.7% to 19.4%. Against a cost of capital assumed at roughly 8% nominal, the business clears it, and it cleared it by more a decade ago.

4. Competitive landscape and market sizing

4.1 Orthopaedics: a four-player oligopoly in which Stryker is the only one gaining

Three of the four majors independently describe the same structure. Stryker's 10-K names Zimmer, Johnson & Johnson MedTech and Smith & Nephew; Zimmer Biomet names the identical three in reverse▪; Smith+Nephew says "we are one of four leading players, competing against US-based companies Stryker, Zimmer Biomet and DePuy Synthes". That agreement is stronger evidence of the structure than any third-party study.

Market sizing is built from the four companies' own filings and cross-checked against Smith+Nephew's published estimate, which sizes Hip and Knee Implants at $17.6bn in 2025, up 5%, with "Others" at 16%.

The trauma-and-extremities table mixes scopes and should be used with that caveat. The Zimmer Biomet comparable retains craniomaxillofacial, roughly 21% of S.E.T. or about $451m, which Stryker reports inside Neuro Cranial rather than Trauma and Extremities; the J&J line excludes shoulders, which J&J reports inside a $2,852m "Spine, Sports & Other" line and never breaks out, and Smith+Nephew's own estimate for J&J including shoulders is 23%. The Stryker, Zimmer and Smith+Nephew figures match Smith+Nephew's independent estimates.

Extremities is the one place a competitor is credibly taking share from Stryker.▪ Zimmer Biomet disclosed that "more than 1/3 of surgeons implanting our Identity total shoulder were using competitive systems 2 years ago", and gave two different figures for its stemless shoulder in successive quarters — "40% of OsseoFit stemless shoulder users are new to Zimmer Biomet" (Q2 2025 call) and "80% of users were competitive accounts" (Q3 2025 call). Neither call names Stryker or Tornier, so attributing those conversions to Stryker's shoulder franchise is an inference from the fact that Tornier is the largest named competitive system in that market, not a disclosure. Stryker's counter is Mako Shoulder, in limited release through 2025 and full commercial launch on Mako 4 in Q2 2026.

Counter-evidence, ranked by how much it changes the structure.

  • Zimmer Biomet's robotics roadmap could change the basis of technical competition: mBos is targeted at "early 2027 ... swiftly follow[ed] by the fully autonomous platform at the end of 2027 or early 2028" (ZBH Q3 2025 call).
  • A separated DePuy Synthes could be a sharper competitor than the J&J division was. The FY2025 drag was explicitly restructuring disruption now "substantially complete", the FY2025 pre-tax charge of $307m falls to $17m by Q2 2026, and Q2 2026 operational growth of 4.2% is already four times the FY2025 rate. Any model extrapolating 1.1% for DePuy Synthes is wrong.
  • Zimmer Biomet's US sales-force rebuild helps Stryker in 2026 and becomes a threat in 2027.
  • Handheld robotics commoditizes the entry point, and Stryker's own RPS targets "a subset of surgeons that are not ready to move all the way to Mako", which is also a segment where the installed-base advantage does not apply.
  • The fragmented tail is compounding faster than the majors: Enovis Reconstructive grew 8.2% organic in FY2025 to $1,111m.

4.2 MedSurg and Neurotechnology: leader on scale in the disclosed lines, third in the one sub-market with a published share table

Stryker's 10-K describes each line as an oligopoly of five to seven named global participants. Three of the seven Endoscopy competitors (Karl Storz, Olympus, Arthrex) and two of the five Medical competitors (Medline, Ferno-Washington) file nothing with the SEC, and Zoll sits inside Asahi Kasei without a disclosed segment, so no clean concentration measure is derivable for any line.

Instruments. Stryker's Orthopaedic Instruments line annualises to roughly $2,024m-$2,092m [estimate: the Q2 2026 10-Q discloses $523m and $501m for the quarter and $1,012m/$985m for six months; H1x2 and Q2x4 bracket the range], against CONMED's entire orthopedic surgery product line of $574.6m and Medtronic's Cranial & Spinal Technologies division of $5,222m, which is far broader because it contains spine implants and biologics. Stryker's Surgical Technologies unit "crossed $1 billion this year" (Q4 2025 call), the only figure ever given for it. Growth comparisons here are not like-for-like: what Stryker now labels "Instruments" is 68% Neuro Cranial by revenue after the recast, so it cannot be compared to a peer's instruments line.

Endoscopy. Stryker's core visualization franchise is roughly $2,497m [estimate: Endoscopy $3,807m less ~$910m sports medicine and ~$400m reprocessing; range $2,400-2,600m] growing 11-12%. Olympus's Surgical & Interventional Solutions Division, the nearest scaled comparator, reported revenue of Y313,109m for the year to 31 March 2026, about $2,076m at Olympus's own Y150.77 rate, down 3.0%, with an operating loss of Y14,986m against a Y15,265m profit the prior year, citing China "where the competitive environment is becoming increasingly intense mainly due to the impact of policies favoring domestic products", plus product ship-holds and a voluntary recall (olympus-global.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web]. Stryker Endoscopy grew 11.7% to $1,004m in the June-2026 quarter, which is a different period from Olympus's fiscal year and is not an overlapping comparison. Smith+Nephew's Arthroscopic Enabling Technologies, the direct like-for-like against Stryker's camera platform, was $647m growing 1.6% underlying.

Part of the recent Endoscopy share gain comes from a competitor's regulatory failure rather than from Stryker's own position. The FDA issued import alerts on 2025-06-24 covering 58 Olympus device models from the Aizu facility, affecting about 1% of Olympus consolidated revenue (medtechdive.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web], and Olympus's FY2026 GAAP operating profit declined 40.2% to Y97.1bn, a 9.6% margin. Stryker's Endoscopy US organic growth was 11.1% in Q4 2025 and 10.2% in Q2 2026. The affected Olympus lines are about 1% of its revenue, so this does not explain most of Stryker's growth; it is a transient share-transfer source that will not repeat, and the same regulatory mechanism could apply to Stryker.

Sports medicine is the one sub-market inside Endoscopy with a filing-sourced share table, and it is where Stryker is not the leader. Smith+Nephew sizes it at $7.0bn in 2025 growing 6% and gives Arthrex 35%, Smith+Nephew 25%, Stryker 13%, DePuy Synthes 9% and others 18%▪, stating that "Smith+Nephew holds a leading position behind Arthrex, and also competes against Stryker and DePuy Synthes" (SNN 20-F FY2025). Stryker's implied ~$910m position is 37% of Arthrex's and 52% of Smith+Nephew's. Arthrex is private, so this is not a position Stryker can buy. A $2.45bn sports-medicine business would also be a competition-review problem even if it were for sale.

Medical. Against the only listed comparator that discloses the line, Stryker Medical at $4,204m is 2.2x Baxter's Care and Connectivity Solutions at $1,911m, and grew 13.4% in Q2 2026 against Baxter's 5%.▪ Zoll's undisclosed scale is the material blind spot: it is the incumbent in hospital defibrillation and wearable cardioverter defibrillators, and Asahi Kasei's segment reporting does not size it.

Vascular. The competitive gap is closing fastest here. Penumbra's thrombectomy line grew 12.5% to $259.0m in calendar Q2 2026 and 18.3% on a two-year CAGR, while Stryker Vascular declined 0.7% reported and 6.7% in the United States in the same quarter.▪ Two pieces of evidence pull in opposite directions on whether that is supply or share. Toward supply: management attributed it entirely to "one plant in the Inari business which frankly makes virtually most of the products" and put the drag at $33m-$49m [estimate: 50-75bps of Q2 2026 net sales of $6,589m]. Toward share: three quarters earlier, before any supply problem, "Vascular had U.S. organic sales growth of 4.3% ... offset by competitive pressures in our ischemic business" (Q4 2025 call). The supply failure is separate from and additional to a share problem Stryker had already named.

4.3 Where the company's own market framing is marketing

The $6bn-plus US venous thromboembolism opportunity is a conversion thesis, not an addressable device pool. Stryker's own Investor Day slide breaks it into a $2.6bn pulmonary-embolism segment where mechanical thrombectomy is 19% ($470m), catheter-directed lytics 2% ($50m) and conservative therapy 79%; a $3.0bn deep-vein-thrombosis segment where mechanical thrombectomy is 14% ($400m), lytics 1% ($12m) and conservative therapy 85%; plus $1bn of chronic venous disease. The internal arithmetic is consistent. What it means is that the device revenue actually spent in the two core indications today is $932m, and the remaining roughly $5bn is patients receiving anticoagulation, compression or systemic thrombolytics valued as if each converted to a device procedure at current prices.▪ Stryker's own presenter said as much: "our competitor is actually conservative therapy". Converting it requires randomised evidence shifting guideline-level standard of care, which is slower and more binary than taking share from a competing device. Penumbra's 10-K supplies an independent patient-count check on the same market: approximately 150,000 US pulmonary-embolism patients are high- or intermediate-risk and thrombectomy-eligible annually, and approximately 350,000 US deep-vein thromboses are eligible.

The weighted-average served-market growth rate of 6% is Stryker's own internal research (Investor Day 2025 deck, slide 16, footnote 2) and the outgrowth measured against it is not independently reconstructable. Within MedSurg the outgrowth ranges from roughly 600-700bps in Endoscopy and Medical to negative in Vascular; the spread across four disclosed lines in a single quarter was 1,480bps, from Medical's +13.0% constant currency to Vascular's -1.8%. The independently sourced orthopaedic-market numbers are Smith+Nephew's +5% for hips and knees and +7% for trauma and extremities, and Stryker's own forward framing on the Q1 2026 call is 200-300bps of outgrowth against the orthopaedic market, not 400.

5. Value chain and profit pools

Stryker's 10-K names no supplier at all. Item 1A describes the supply base only by function: sole-source suppliers of raw materials, components and finished devices; third-party sterilization service providers; electronic-component suppliers. Downstream, the 10-K names no 10%-or-greater customer and no group purchasing organisation. The layers below are therefore built from the filings of the companies that occupy those functions industry-wide, and are layer economics rather than Stryker's own suppliers.

For a Medicare primary lower-extremity joint replacement the facility payment averaged $13,696 per episode in 2023 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, accessed 2026-07-31) [web], and the 2026 national Medicare ambulatory-surgery-centre rate for a total knee replacement is $9,393 (datalilyai.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web]. A systematic review puts the mean standard knee implant at $5,336 plus or minus $1,671, or 22.3% of the $23,907 mean total cost of a primary knee replacement (jorthobusiness.org, accessed 2026-07-31) [web].

Layer Named companies with filings Revenue capture Gross / segment margin Who sets price at this interface
Specialty alloys (Ti, CoCr) Carpenter Technology Medical end-use sales $351.2m FY2025, (6)% Consolidated GM 26.7% The mill. A surcharge passes raw-material cost through, and Carpenter still "realized price increases particularly in the orthopedic and dental sub-markets"
Contract manufacture of devices Integer Holdings Sales $1,853.6m FY2025 GM 27.0% The OEM. Thin, cost-plus
Outsourced terminal sterilization Sotera Health (Sterigenics); STERIS (AST) Sterigenics ~$755.8m; STERIS AST $1,138.5m Sterigenics segment income 54.6%; STERIS AST operating margin 46.1% The sterilizer. Both raised price in the latest year; ethylene oxide and cobalt-60 are single-sourced
Stryker SYK Net sales $25,116m FY2025 GM 64.0%; segment operating margins 29.9% and 29.8%; GAAP operating margin 19.5% Stryker, at the margin, and only recently

Acute hospital HCA, Tenet hospitals, UHS HCA revenue $75,600m FY2025 HCA supplies 15.0% of revenue Hospital and GPO
Ambulatory surgery centre Tenet Ambulatory Care (USPI), Surgery Partners USPI segment revenue ~$5,180m, +14.1% USPI supplies 26.6% of revenue (26.2% FY2024) The ASC, increasingly
Payor UnitedHealth, Elevance UNH medical care ratio 89.1% FY2025 Payor retains ~10.9% of premium The payor sets the facility payment

Three things follow. Stryker is not the highest-margin layer in its own chain: outsourced sterilization, a mandatory and FDA-validated step for essentially every implant and sterile disposable Stryker ships and a dependency Stryker names by function in its own risk factors, earns 46-55% operating or segment-income margins against Stryker's 19.5% consolidated GAAP operating margin.▪ The layers Stryker could in-source are the low-margin ones: contract manufacture at a 27.0% gross margin and specialty alloy at 26.7% buy volume, not margin, which is consistent with what Stryker says it is doing. And distribution has been squeezed to 1.1%, which is why the direct model is worth roughly the whole distribution layer's margin and why the 10-K flags dealer defection as a distinct risk.

The binding constraint is Stryker's own capacity, at the capital and new-launch end only. Item 1A states flatly: "In certain instances we have been unable to meet demand due to supply chain challenges, which has led to loss of sales." On the Pangea trauma launch: "We just have to make the product as fast as we can. They're very complex kits ... they take many quarters to be fully launched" (Q1 2026 call). The Q1 2026 cyber incident is the cleanest natural experiment — manufacturing stopped for almost three weeks, manufacturing and supply-chain costs took 200bps out of Q1 gross margin, orders did not pause, and the revenue moved right rather than disappearing. It is not a constraint on the mature implant base: 214 days of inventory is not the pattern of a company that cannot make enough; it is the pattern of consignment, in which Stryker funds roughly seven months of finished goods across the customer base so no case is lost for want of the right size. The regulated switching cost at the supplier interface is measurable: product transfers "used to take us about 3 years or so on average" and now run "anywhere from 6 months for a simple product to about 18 months to a very complex product" (Investor Day 2025-11-13).

Bargaining power moved to Stryker upstream and is disputed downstream. Upstream the mechanism is disclosed: product transfer at scale, dual sourcing and in-sourcing from suppliers into Stryker plants, with the network going from about 44 plants plus 22 acquired down to 42 today and 70% of US-sold product made in the US. The financial trace is the gross-margin bridge line for manufacturing and supply-chain costs, which went (360)bps into 2022, then (40)bps, (40)bps and 0bps into 2025. The counter-evidence is that Carpenter took price from orthopaedics in FY2025 in the same year Stryker claimed its best product cost reduction in a decade; both can be true because Stryker's savings come from network consolidation rather than from beating the mills, but the input cost line is not falling. Tariffs are the involuntary version of the same interface: an estimated $175-200m net cost in 2025, then a $158m credit booked in Q2 2026 for "Reversal of 2025 tariffs", worth 240bps of gross margin on the quarter's $6,589m of net sales.

Downstream, Stryker won on unit price and the hospital won on total spend. HCA cut supplies from 16.5% of revenue in 2018-2019 to 15.0% in 2025 and 14.3% in Q2 2026 — 220bps of the customer's revenue line reclaimed from the supply chain over seven years, a larger transfer than the 100-150bps of price Stryker recovered.▪ HCA's own decomposition for FY2025 shows device cost per equivalent admission up 7.0% against total revenue per equivalent admission up 4.0%, so devices did outpace revenue in 2025; in Q2 2026 device cost per equivalent admission was +0.1% and total supply cost per equivalent admission declined 1.0%. In the same quarter HCA's outpatient surgeries declined 4.4% and inpatient surgeries 2.3% while Stryker reported +9.0% organic. Site-of-care migration, mix and international explain the direction, but it is the sharpest divergence between Stryker's growth and its largest customer channel's volumes in the period examined.

The ASC channel pays the same implant price out of a much smaller payment, and the evidence on the net effect cuts both ways. Tenet's USPI runs supplies at 26.6% of revenue and rising, against 15.0% in Tenet's hospital segment, because an ASC collects a fraction of the acute payment for the same procedure while paying substantially the same implant price. Stryker's own exposure is "mid-teens right now of our joint business that goes through ASCs" (Investor Day 2025-11-13). Every point of that mix shift moves Stryker's dollar into a customer whose device spend is already more than a quarter of revenue and who has no cross-subsidy from inpatient room-and-board. The shift raises Stryker's volume and pressures its price, and the deciding fact — the price and gross-margin differential between an ASC placement and a hospital placement — is not disclosed anywhere.

Customer-side economics of a Mako. At disclosed utilization and business-line revenue, Mako-attached knee and hip implant revenue is roughly $1,701m across more than 3,000 systems, about $567k of implant revenue per system per year [estimate: global knees $2,656m x 50% plus global hips $1,865m x 20%, divided by >3,000 systems; range $500-620k allowing for the "over" qualifiers], or roughly $4.0m over a seven-year life before system and service revenue. What it costs the buyer is not disclosed by Stryker. Trade press from 2017 puts the system at $1.0-1.25m, annual service at about $100k and incremental disposables at about $1,000 a case (medcitynews.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web]. On those inputs a full-size Mako running 300 cases a year costs the facility about $557k a year, or $1,857 a case [estimate: $1.1m capital straight-lined over seven years plus $100k service plus $1,000/case disposables; the cost inputs date from 2017 and are an order of magnitude, not a current quote]. Against the $9,393 Medicare ambulatory payment, the $5,336 mean implant plus the robot consume $7,193, or 77% of the payment, before staff, facility or anaesthesia.▪ That is what explains Mako RPS and why management describes the ASC opportunity as concentrated in "new builds and big renovations" rather than conversion of the installed base.

The documented economic benefit of robotic knee replacement accrues to the payor, not the buyer of the robot.▪ A published economic analysis of a commercially insured under-65 cohort reports 90-day global expenditures of $28,204 for robotic-assisted against $32,253 for manual, post-surgery expenditures of $6,857 against $8,189, and skilled-nursing-facility use of 1.68% against 6.05% (ajmc.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web]. Under fee-for-service every dollar of that saving lands with the payor; the hospital pays for the robot and its return has to come from surgeon recruitment and volume share. That changed on 1 January 2026, when CMS's Transforming Episode Accountability Model began — mandatory, five years, 741 acute-care hospitals across 188 metropolitan areas covering roughly 25% of Medicare beneficiaries, with lower-extremity joint replacement the largest of five episodes (cms.gov, accessed 2026-07-31) [web]. It cuts both ways: it converts length-of-stay and skilled-nursing savings into money the hospital keeps, and it puts the implant inside the hospital's target price, giving a hospital at 30-day episode risk a sharper reason to negotiate down the $5,336 implant.

Financing. Stryker's Note 2 discloses that it sells customer lease agreements and the related leased assets to third-party financial institutions without recourse, and that revenue under those arrangements was "less than 4% of our total revenue for 2025, 2024 and 2023". The paragraph did not exist before the FY2024 10-K, and the threshold moved from "less than 3%" to "less than 4%" in one year across three overlapping years. A 4% ceiling on FY2025 revenue is up to about $1.0bn of capital placed on lease paper Stryker originates and then sells. That has three consequences: up to a billion dollars a year of what is described as hospital capital demand is third-party lessor credit arranged at the point of sale; the proceeds are classified as operating cash flow, which flatters the free-cash-flow conversion ratio against a peer that holds the paper; and while the credit risk does leave, the demand dependency does not, because if lessor appetite or rates move the order book converts more slowly regardless of hospital demand.

6. Secular and industry trends

6.1 Growth attribution: what the realised record shows

Stryker splits organic growth into unit volume and price every year, and that split cuts against the claim that growth structurally accelerated.

Average organic growth over 2016-2019 was 7.4% and over 2023-2025 was 10.7%, an acceleration of 329bps. Average price moved from (1.20)% to +0.70%, worth 190bps or 58% of that acceleration. Average unit volume moved from 8.58% to 9.97%, worth 139bps or 42%.▪ The price contribution has already ended: +1.1% (FY2024), +0.4% (FY2025), +0.3% (Q1 2026), 0.0% (Q2 2026). FY2026 guidance of 8.3-9.3% organic with modestly positive price implies unit volume of roughly 8.0-9.0%. Stryker realised 7.8-9.3% unit volume in 2016-2019, at a third of today's revenue, before Mako scaled from a few hundred systems to over 3,000 and before roughly 60 acquisitions. The durable, volume-driven part of the acceleration is roughly 140bps at its peak and close to zero against the guided year. One qualification cuts the same way: the unit-volume bucket absorbs mix, so a shift toward higher-priced products is counted as volume and true unit growth is lower. A second point bears on the comparison rather than on the direction — the FY2026 guide is clean because management did not reduce the year for the cyber event: the January guide midpoint was 8.75% and the narrowed midpoint is 8.80%.
