Knees plus Hips, the whole Mako-pulled implant business, generated $353m, 15.3% of the $2,300m of ongoing dollars added. Trauma and Extremities alone generated more, and its drivers are the Wright Medical shoulder portfolio and the Pangea plating launch, not Mako.▪

The Mako test. Knee revenue compounded at 6.6% over 2015-2019 and 6.5% over 2019-2025, across the period in which the installed base passed 3,000 systems in 45-plus countries, US knee utilization reached over two-thirds and cumulative procedures passed two million.▪ Measured from 2021 instead, the same line compounded 9.5% over 2021-2025. Hips did improve materially, from 2.3% to 5.1%, consistent with Mako Hip being the later-penetrating application and with the Insignia stem launch. The two windows differ because of what they contain rather than what the robot did: 2019-2025 contains the COVID collapse and the rebound off it and is the through-cycle comparison, while 2021-2025 starts after the collapse and measures the rebound. This does not show Mako is worthless: the counterfactual, knee revenue without Mako, is unobservable, and defending a 6.5% growth rate against three well-capitalised competitors may itself be the achievement. It does mean the disclosed record does not support treating Mako penetration as an accelerant of the joint-replacement business's revenue growth rate.

Against industry dollars and a peer cohort. In FY2025 Stryker grew like a strong reconstruction peer plus roughly 400-500bps: Knees +8.2% and Hips +8.9% constant currency against Zimmer Biomet's FY2025 organic constant currency of +3.9% and J&J MedTech Orthopaedics' Q1 2026 operational +3.2%. By Q2 2026 that premium had narrowed sharply in the flagship lines: US Knees +6.2% against a cohort running 2-5%, and US Hips +4.9% against Smith+Nephew's +5.8% and J&J's +3.5%, so Stryker's hips now grow in line with or below the peer group.▪ Management's answer was a comparable-base argument and "one quarter doesn't make a trend", which is fair and is not evidence of continued outgrowth. In the adjacency cohort Stryker is losing outright: it paid $4,810m net of cash for Inari to enter a US market it sizes at over $6bn, Inari grew high-single to low-double digits in FY2025, and Penumbra compounded 17.5% in FY2025 with US venous thromboembolism revenue up 34% in Q3 2025.

An independent test of the outgrowth claim, built from a constant panel of 27 medtech companies with unbroken data, gives a median outgrowth of +470bps over 2012-2025, +298bps over 2016-2019 and +563bps over 2021-2025. On that benchmark the claim is conservative rather than promotional. The caveat is that the panel is revenue-weighted and therefore dominated by J&J, Abbott, Medtronic and Philips, whose median growth of 2.5% is well below any reasonable definition of the medtech market. A slower panel is an easier benchmark, so the +470bps median outgrowth flatters every company measured against it, Stryker included. Stryker's share of that panel's revenue went from 4.0% in 2011 to 7.1% in 2025, a gain of 310bps over fourteen years, most of it in the last five.

Recomputed from a pre-COVID base, compounding the disclosed organic rates from 2019 gives 59.4% cumulative growth over six years, an 8.1% organic CAGR. Against the 6% weighted-average served-market growth rate that is roughly 205bps of outgrowth▪; against the 4%-to-6% range averaged over the period, roughly 300bps, which is the number management itself quoted in November 2023. The 100bps of apparent improvement between the 2023 and 2025 Investor Days is an artefact of the starting year.

6.2 Separating the durable from the cyclical

Structural. Four drivers are structural: fragility-fracture incidence, which is demographic and non-elective and which the 2020 test isolates cleanly; penetration of arthroplasty into joints that were previously not replaced, particularly shoulder and foot and ankle; CMS penalty-driven infection-prevention purchases, which are cost-avoidance decisions priced against a regulatory penalty rather than discretionary capital; and the site-of-care shift into ambulatory centres, rate-limited by construction rather than demand.

Cyclical. Two drivers are cyclical: hospital and ambulatory capital budgets, which fund the majority of MedSurg revenue and are at a high that is starting to turn; and elective large-joint volume, which is deferrable, with a 2020 amplitude of a 13.7% decline in Knees and a 123% decremental margin at the segment.

Shifts that flatten the slope.

  • The CY2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule proposed rule would cut physician reimbursement for total hip and knee replacement by up to 20% in 2027, on top of an 8% cut to joint-replacement surgeon reimbursement effective 2026, with comments due 14 September 2026 (beckersspine.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web]. This does not cut Stryker's implant price directly, because implants are paid through facility rates. The mechanism runs through the surgeon: Stryker's orthopaedic demand pull is surgeon preference, and the 10-K names as a distinct risk the loss of "working relationships with the healthcare professionals who assist in product development". A fee cut of that size pushes independent surgeons into hospital employment or larger groups, and employed surgeons lose implant-choice autonomy to value-analysis committees and group purchasing organisations. Management's answer was that proposed rules "create noise" and settle at "a reasonable place".
  • GLP-1 receptor agonists. A study published 2 June 2026 links their use to a reduced eight-year likelihood of knee replacement, with a 1-year absolute risk reduction of 1.44% after three years of treatment translating to roughly 14,400 fewer US total knee replacements a year (bmjgroup.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web]. That is about 1.4% of annual volume against a base compounding at roughly 5.9%, and it is partly offset because lower BMI expands the population eligible for ambulatory procedures.
  • EU medical-device regulation is already visible: "Europe's growth, which was high single low double digit for many years has slipped into kind of the 6%-ish percent range because Insignia ... is not on the market yet. Pangea is not on the market yet" (Investor Day 2025-11-13), and Stryker is now launching in Japan before Europe.
  • China's volume-based procurement is named in the 10-K and sized nowhere.

Shifts that steepen it.

  • Total ankle reimbursement rose more than 50% from 1 January 2026 in both the ambulatory and hospital settings, against the Incompass Total Ankle launch.
  • PEERLESS II is the single largest identifiable upside to the slope of any Stryker end market, and it is binary and dated: FlowTriever against anticoagulation alone in over 1,200 patients, enrolment complete, readout mid-2027, targeting the roughly 85% of pulmonary-embolism patients on conservative therapy.
  • Mako Shoulder and Mako RPS both moved to full US commercial launch in the first half of 2026, with the shoulder market-expansion thesis unevidenced by management's own account: "I'm a big believer. Now I have no data, so this is anecdotal."

Peak-to-peak is the only usable comparison, because 2020 was an exogenous shutdown rather than a cycle trough. Organic growth was 8.1% in 2019, 10.3% in 2025 and guided at 8.3-9.3% for 2026; unit volume was 9.0% in 2019 and about 8.0-9.0% implied for 2026.▪ Organic growth in the guided year is back within about 100bps of the 2019 rate and unit volume is at or below it. The 2023-2025 bulge was the coincidence of a procedure-backlog recovery and the only sustained period of positive medtech pricing in Stryker's disclosed history.

7. Critical points

1. The second half of 2026 has to grow roughly 11% organically and the evidence for it is an adjective. H1 2026 organic growth was 5.8% (Q1 +2.4% on the cyber shutdown, Q2 +9.0%). Weighting by prior-year half revenue, the 8.8% full-year midpoint requires about 11.5% in H2, the largest half-over-half acceleration Stryker has ever guided to▪; an analyst put it at "about 11%" on the Q2 2026 call and management did not dispute it. On earnings, H1 adjusted EPS of $6.29 leaves $8.66-$8.81 for H2, up 13.1-15.0% on H2 2025's $7.66. The entire stated support is a capital order book described as "elevated" with "0 cancellations" in three consecutive calls. The word "backlog" appears zero times in the FY2024 and FY2025 10-Ks, there is no remaining-performance-obligation disclosure, and the one balance-sheet handle went the wrong way: contract liabilities declined $27m in H1 2026 to $997m after net additions of +$118m in 2024 and +$46m in 2025.

2. Price, the largest single change in the composition of Stryker's growth in a decade, has already reversed. Price contribution to consolidated growth was negative in every one of the nine years 2014-2022, cumulatively taking about 10.8 points off constant-currency growth, then turned positive in 2023 and added 2.1 points back over three years. Quarterly, it peaked at +1.2% in Q3 2024 and printed 0.0% in Q2 2026, the first quarter in three years with none. Orthopaedics has shown 0bps in its segment margin bridge for four consecutive reporting periods. On a $25.1bn base, a return to the pre-2023 regime of roughly -1.2% a year would take about 160bps a year off growth and, at close to full flow-through, more than erase the margin expansion both management and consensus expect.

3. Mako drives share, not revenue growth or price. Over 2019-2025 the installed base passed 3,000 systems, US knee utilization reached over two-thirds and cumulative procedures passed two million, while knee revenue compounded at 6.5% against 6.6% in the four preceding years; on the post-COVID 2021-2025 window it compounded 9.5%. Over FY2022-25 the two Mako-exposed lines compounded 9.9% against 10.8% for the ex-spine segment, and they are the two slowest lines in H1 2026. Share did move — roughly 191bps of the four-player hip-and-knee pool over 2023-2025 — and price did stop eroding. Both are real; neither is the acceleration the framing implies. Mako plus enabling technologies and bone cement is about 6% of the restated Orthopaedics segment and Mako alone is less, and in the forward model a 150bps-a-year change in the growth rate of Knees and Hips moves 2033 operating income by 1.8%, the smallest of the five revenue drivers.

4. The Q1 2026 recast makes almost every historical segment comparison invalid, and it removed the last segment return-on-capital denominator. Roughly $2.0bn a year of Orthopaedic Instruments moved from MedSurg into a new Ortho Tech line inside Orthopaedics; Neuro Cranial and spine Enabling Technologies moved into Instruments; $518m of goodwill was reallocated on a relative-fair-value basis, creating a new reporting unit.▪ What moved out of MedSurg was the power-tool franchise, not Mako, which already sat in Orthopaedics. The reported split shifts from 62.3/37.7 to 54.2/45.8. Of the apparent 420bps step in Orthopaedics margin from FY2025's 29.8% to Q2 2026's 34.0%, roughly 310bps is the recast: like-for-like restated H1 improvement was 40bps and the Q2 improvement 90bps. From Q1 2026 Stryker also stopped disclosing segment assets, so FY2025 is the last year in which any segment return on capital can be computed.

5. The one business Stryker has never disclosed is its most profitable. Differencing two filings for the same six months prices the transferred bundle at a 47.2% segment operating margin on a 64.4% gross margin and 8.6% of revenue in SG&A, against the implant business at 28.6% on a 73.3% gross margin and 34.5% SG&A. Power tools and their per-case disposables attach to every case regardless of implant vendor and need no per-case rep. The highest-margin unit is power tools rather than implants.

6. Vascular is the line Stryker markets hardest and the one that has performed worst. After removing Inari, Vascular contributed roughly 4% of MedSurg's FY2023-25 organic growth on 13% of its revenue. Management named "competitive pressures in our ischemic business" in Q4 2025, before any supply problem. Q2 2026 was -0.7% reported, -1.8% constant currency and -6.7% in the United States. Against that, Peripheral Vascular goodwill of $3,203m was tested quantitatively at 31 October 2025 with fair value exceeding carrying amount by 12% — every other reporting unit passed qualitatively — and the precedent is Spine, which had 10% headroom at the October 2023 test and took $456m of impairment fourteen months later.

7. Returns on invested capital have fallen by about two-thirds since 2010 and the recovery is one five-year window. On a normalized 21% tax, ROIC went from 36.3% (2010) to 7.2% (2020) to 11.9% (2025) — fifteen years, not ten. Over the ten years the Section 13.1 series on a normalized 15% tax runs 17.2% (2016) to 13.0% (2025), a 24% decline. Incremental returns by five-year window were 1.9% (2010-15), 1.8% (2015-20) and 20.7% (2020-25). The 2015-2020 window absorbed Sage, Physio-Control, K2M, Entellus and Wright Medical and converted $16,055m of incremental invested capital into $286m of incremental NOPAT. The forward question is which regime the next $24bn of deployable cash resembles; the reference class cleared 10% incremental ROIC in only 37% of five-year windows above $5bn of revenue.

8. Growth at this scale is close to unprecedented inside medical devices. In 49 medtech company-years starting above $20bn of revenue since 2005, the median forward five-year revenue CAGR was 1.3%, p75 3.7% and p90 7.8%, and 10% reached 8%. All five instances of 8%-plus compounding from above $20bn are Abbott windows spanning a goodwill step from $7,683m to $24,020m. Consensus asks Stryker for 8.5% over 2025-2028 and models zero acquisition contribution. The offsetting fact is that Stryker has not decayed with scale: its trailing three-year CAGR was 10.8% at $25bn against 7.2% at $9bn in 2013, and it bought its growth more cheaply than almost anyone in the class that achieved it — $0.61 of goodwill per $1 of revenue added over 2020-2025 against a class median of $1.14.

9. The 2026 de-rating happened without a change in estimates. FY2026 consensus adjusted EPS moved from $15.013 on 2026-03-31, three weeks after the cyber attack, to $14.996 on 2026-07-31, a net -0.1%; FY2027 moved -0.2% and FY2028 -0.05%. Over the same window the price declined 1.6%, and from the 2026-02-27 intra-year high of $387.46 it declined 16.5%. Since the November-2024 peak, forward EPS rose 19.7% and the forward multiple contracted 31.1%. Twenty-seven analysts occupy a FY2026 EPS band 2.7% wide, straddling management's own guidance range, while target prices span 47.6%. The disagreement priced into the stock is not about next year's earnings.

10. Two large contingent exposures sit outside the operating business. The German Federal Central Tax Office has issued assessments of $754m for 2010-2017 with a further $11m expected, against $403m of total company-wide unrecognized tax benefits, and Stryker left the reserve for the matter unchanged after receiving the assessment. EY made it a critical audit matter. Separately, the March 2026 cyber incident was destructive rather than extortive: reporting attributes it to a group linked to Iranian state intelligence and to abuse of the device-management platform rather than to ransomware, which removes the negotiated-restore option and makes recurrence a function of geopolitics. Stryker's own Q1 2026 10-Q now names "the United States' ongoing combat operations in Iran" as a cyber-threat driver.

8. Management claim pressure tests

The 400bps outgrowth claim is measured against a benchmark Stryker defines and has revised upward, and the FY2026 guide assumes 200-300bps. Management's framing at the November 2025 Investor Day is a 10% compound growth rate since 2020, 400bps faster than a weighted-average served-market growth rate that "moved from 4% to 6%", with the move attributed to acquiring into faster-growing spaces. Two years earlier the same metric was "300 basis points faster than the market" against end markets described as "roughly mid-single-digit growth". Both the numerator and the company-defined denominator rose between the two events. Recomputed from a pre-COVID 2019 base, organic growth was 8.1% a year, which against a 6% market is roughly 205bps. And the mix explanation does not survive its own arithmetic: the disclosed 9-point shift out of hips and knees produces roughly 81bps of weighted-average uplift at a generous 9-point growth-rate gap between the exiting and receiving categories, not the 200bps claimed▪ [estimate: 0.09 x 0.09 = 81bps; producing 200bps would require a 22-point gap]. The residual is the served markets themselves growing faster post-COVID. Management's own forward number is lower: FY2026 guidance "assumes we will continue to outgrow the orthopaedic marketplace by 200 to 300 basis points, just as we have in the last few years", which asserts continuity rather than a step-down, but sits against a 2025 record of roughly 390bps in hip and knee and 560bps in trauma and extremities on Smith+Nephew's market map.

Management describes pricing as a structural capability; it has gone to zero. "Our commission rates are set based on pricing or discount level. So our sales professionals are inspired ... to be part of the solution and driving better pricing. That's why you've seen us improve pricing over time. It will continue to be that way" (Investor Day 2025-11-13). The CFO on the Q4 2025 call: "we're building price gains on top of price gains from before ... we expect 2026 to look pretty similar from a price standpoint to 2025." The FY2025 10-K attributes -0.1% to lower prices in Orthopaedics and the entire consolidated +0.4% price benefit to MedSurg. MedSurg's contribution then went +0.7% (FY2025) to +0.3% (H1 2026) to +0.1% (Q2 2026), and the Q2 2026 segment margin bridge has no pricing line at all. A 160bp swing in MedSurg price contribution over three years is roughly $250m of annualized revenue at zero incremental cost, or about 160bps of segment operating margin, and it has already reversed. The filing wins over the spoken claim.

MedSurg is presented as the source of operating leverage and five years of segment data show none. Management points to two consecutive years of at least 100bps of adjusted operating margin expansion, 200bps promised and delivered over three years, and a further minimum 150bps through 2028.▪ At the MedSurg segment level, operating margin was 28.9% in FY2020 and 29.9% in FY2025 on 88% more revenue, and the incremental operating margin across that whole span was 30.9%, within a point of the 29.9% average margin.▪ FY2022's incremental margin was -6.5%. Restated H1 2026 segment margin is 25.2% against 25.2% a year earlier. The company-level margin expansion is real; it is disproportionately Orthopaedics (27.2% to 29.8% over 2023-25) plus corporate discipline rather than MedSurg scaling.

FY2025's Orthopaedics margin expansion was portfolio pruning, not leverage. Reported segment margin rose 130bps to 29.8%. Ex-Spinal Implants, the ongoing business's margin was -59bps if the divested unit earned 0% and -123bps if it earned -10%▪, and it is positive only if Spinal Implants was earning close to +10% — implausible for a business Stryker impaired $456m of goodwill against in 2024 and then wrote down a further $362m to fair value less cost to sell. The same arithmetic supplies the FY2026 expansion for free, because Spinal Implants runs off from $185m to roughly $10m.

The recurring-revenue framing is bounded far below what the SmartHospital marketing implies, and management will not size it. Under 10% of company sales are recognised as services over time, so under $2,512m company-wide against restated MedSurg of about $13,760m [estimate: FY2025 as-reported $15,647m less a full year of Orthopaedic Instruments (~$2,020m) plus Enabling Technologies (~$130m); range $13,600-13,900m]. Contract liabilities are $1,024m, about 7.4% of a year's segment revenue, and the balance declined $27m in H1 2026 with net additions decelerating for two consecutive periods. Asked at the Investor Day whether the SaaS revenue inside Medical could be shared, the CFO said "We don't share today beyond that segment of medical what's in that number." Management separately describes the SmartCare portfolio as sold on "a reoccurring software subscription" basis; if subscriptions were scaling, the prepaid book should be building. Management's own quantification of durability, given once, is "~25% capital / ~75% procedurally driven" (Q4 2025 call), which measures something different from the contractual-recurring figure and should not be conflated with it.

The capital order book is being converted against a hospital margin cycle that has already turned. Management's framing is that "demand isn't the problem as it relates to capital equipment. It's really just being able to fulfill those demands". US hospital adjusted year-to-date operating margin closed 2025 at 1.3%, and through May 2026 national hospital operating margins were down 5% year over year with the West down 12% and the Midwest and Great Plains down 7% each [web, Kaufman Hall]. Stryker's 2026 second-half revenue converts an order book written in 2025; the 2027 book is being written against 2026 hospital margins. Stryker's own capital-specific corroboration is European: "a slower capital environment in Europe during the quarter" (Q4 2025 call). Management's Q2 2026 remark about "a slight slowdown in Europe" refers to procedures rather than capital and should not be used for this point.

"Double-digit EPS annually" is not supported by the low end of the company's own guide. Lobo committed at the November 2025 Investor Day to "double-digit EPS annually". Nine weeks later management guided FY2026 adjusted EPS to $14.90-$15.10 against FY2025's $13.63, a range of +9.3% to +10.8%; the Q2 2026 narrowing moved the floor to +9.7%, still short.▪ Delivering the commitment requires at least $14.99. Consensus sits at $14.996, which is $13.63 x 1.10 to within half a cent. The Street is modelling precisely the minimum that satisfies the commitment and none of the historical beat pattern, despite Stryker having beaten the top of its initial EPS range in eight of the last ten guided years by a mean of 1.56%.

Stryker has given two deal-level return standards and reported against neither. On the Wright Medical deal call in November 2019: "We expect ROIC to be greater than 7% by the end of year 5." Year five was 2025, and no ROIC for Wright appears in any 10-K, transcript or investor day. On Inari, the CFO offered "we generally target to get back to WACC sometime between 5 and 7 years", which is a return to the cost of capital rather than above it, over half a decade. Beyond those two, no hurdle rate, IRR target, payback criterion or company-level ROIC figure appears in any 10-K, proxy or deck across the ten years reviewed, and ROIC has never been selected as a compensation metric although it sits in the equity plan's own list of permissible criteria. The discipline is demonstrated by outcomes rather than by a published standard.

Mako is the most consequential asset in Orthopaedics and it has never appeared in the risk factors. Extracting Item 1A from each of the ten 10-Ks from FY2016 to FY2025 returns zero mentions of Mako in all ten years and exactly one "robotics" hit per filing from FY2023, inside the generic competition risk factor. Orthopaedics was $9,469m of FY2025 sales at a 29.8% segment margin, and the Q1 2026 recast added roughly $2bn a year to it. Mako itself is heavily discussed on earnings calls; what is close to absent is any question that names a robotic competitor or asks about robot share. The asymmetry is in the risk disclosure rather than in the analyst dialogue.

The resumed buyback is small against the share count and against free cash flow. The CFO said on 2025-11-13 that "at this point in time, we do not have plans to do any additional share buybacks into the future", and slide 64 of the same deck footnoted "No buybacks have been executed since 2019 and there are no plans to resume activity". On 2026-07-30 the same CFO said "we plan to resume share repurchases this quarter". The remaining authorisation is $1,033m, unchanged since December 2019, which at $323.49 retires 3.19m shares — 0.83% of shares outstanding, 24% of one year's free cash flow and about three years of gross issuance. Both executives conditioned it explicitly on M&A deal flow. It is enough to stop the share count rising for roughly three years.

Five episodes shaped the current company.

  • 2012-2014, the hip recall forced a change of operating philosophy. GAAP operating margin declined from 20.1% (2012) to 12.9% (2014) and diluted EPS from $3.39 to $1.34, with recall charges of $761m in 2014 alone. The choices were to settle early and broadly rather than litigate, to reserve at the actuarially determined low end and top up annually, and to keep spending on acquisitions through it — $2,320m in 2013 and $916m in 2014. The recall was forced; the response was chosen, and it established a pattern repeated in 2020 and 2026: Stryker funds a crisis out of the P&L and does not cut the growth budget.
  • 2013-2018, MAKO took five years to work. Six placements in a quarter in mid-2014, 72 units for full-year 2015, then in Q4 2017 the first visible inflection: 35 installations in the quarter, 42,500 cumulative Mako procedures against 22,000 a year earlier, robots in about 10% of the US customer base, and "our U.S. primary Knee sales and Mako Total Knee accounts grew at 5x the rate of accounts without the Mako Total Knee application". Knee revenue compounded 6.6% over 2015-2019 and 9.5% over 2021-2025, and 6.5% over the through-cycle 2019-2025 window that contains the COVID collapse. Stryker will sit on an underperforming capital platform for four to five years while it rebuilds the sales model around it, and will not talk the asset down in the interim.
  • 2018-2025, the seven-year spine failure. K2M cost $1,380m in November 2018. Spine revenue went from $1,085m (2019) to $1,189m (2023), a 2.3% CAGR while the group compounded about 11%. Write-downs identified: $216m (2022), $273m plus $183m (2024), a $362m valuation allowance (Q4 2024) and roughly $33m more in H1 2025 — about $1,067m in total. In November 2023 Lobo defended keeping the business: "we believe if we can grow something, why would we want to sell something?" Fourteen months later Stryker signed the agreement to sell it. Stryker is slow to concede a failing business and then moves fast, and management's public confidence in a business is a poor leading indicator of what it will do with it.
  • 2021-2025, the organic growth step-change and margin recovery. Organic growth averaged 10.9% across 2021-2025 against 7.4% over 2016-2019, sustained for four years after the rebound year on a base that grew from $14.9bn to $25.1bn. Adjusted operating margin went 23.8% (2022) to 26.3% (2025). The decisions behind it were portfolio rotation through M&A, the spine exit and a formal margin programme. The growth acceleration was at least partly purchased, and the market definition it is measured against is one the company moved itself.
  • 2026, the two operating shocks. The cyber incident and the Inari plant failure both hit supply rather than demand, and both landed in the year in which the guidance depends on production throughput. Q1 2026 was the first adjusted-EPS decline in the transcript record.

10. Management, incentives and capital allocation

Kevin Lobo, 60, has run Stryker for nearly fourteen years, the longest tenure of any large-cap medtech CEO currently serving; net sales went from roughly $8.7bn in 2012 to $25,116m in 2025 and adjusted EPS from roughly $4.06 to $13.63. He dropped the President title on 1 January 2026 when Spencer Stiles, previously Group President Orthopaedics, became President and COO. Preston Wells became CFO on 1 April 2025 in an internal transition pre-announced twelve months ahead, with Glenn Boehnlein moving to an advisory role at unchanged pay and no severance agreement. The bench is internally grown and stable; one named-executive exit in eight years looks like a departure rather than a retirement. The board is ten directors, nine independent, with Sherilyn McCoy as Lead Independent Director and no independent chair. Ronda Stryker, a director since 1984, holds 4.0% of shares.

What management is paid to do. The 2025 annual bonus ran on adjusted operating income (20%), adjusted operating income margin (20%), constant-currency sales (40%) and free cash flow excluding recall payments (20%), gated at 80% of target adjusted operating income, and paid 100.0% of target. Long-term incentives are performance stock units split equally between three-year average adjusted EPS growth and average reported net sales growth relative to a 17-company comparison group, each scoring 0-200%. The annual plan discriminates: Lobo's bonus paid 74.4% of target in 2022, 180.0% in 2023, 135.0% in 2024 and 100.0% in 2025. The long-term plan discriminates on only one of its two halves — across six disclosed cycles the EPS half ranged 74% to 200%, while the relative-sales half paid the 200% maximum in five of six and landed at the 94th percentile or above in five of six.

Four features of the plan design stand out.

  • No return metric. The 2026 proxy contains no reference to return on invested capital, return on capital or total shareholder return as a compensation metric; every metric in both plans is a growth, margin or cash-flow measure.
  • Opposite treatment of acquisitions. The annual plan excludes acquisitions that close after targets are set while the long-term plan measures reported sales growth, which includes them, so short-term pay neutralises acquisitions and long-term pay rewards them.
  • A comparison group that does not compete with Stryker. It is majority diagnostics, life-science tools, dialysis and diversified imaging businesses that mostly grow mid-single-digit or slower, which is why a high-single-digit organic grower lands at the 94th percentile.
  • Adjusted EPS as the pay metric. Its premium to GAAP widened from +33% in 2016 to +62% in 2025, and the largest single 2025 adjustment was $660m of "tax matters", worth $1.71 a share.

Recomputing the 2023 performance-stock-unit EPS metric with the tax line stripped from every year gives a three-year average of 8.0% against a target band of 6.5-8.5%, which pays 100% on that half rather than 200% [estimate: adjusted EPS less the disclosed tax-matters adjustment for 2022-2025; assumes linear interpolation between the top of the band and the maximum, and strips only the tax line]. The difference on Lobo's 2023 grant is 12,583 shares, about $4.4m at the 31 December 2025 close.

Two restraints are real. The 2025 overachievement tranche was gated on adjusted operating income margin measured on a basis that includes acquisitions, divestitures and currency; measured that way the 26.44% target was missed, so all three overachievement measures paid zero and Lobo forfeited up to $2,250,000. And the Committee declined to adjust 2025 payouts for tariffs. Governance hygiene is clean on the items that usually go wrong: no employment, severance or change-in-control agreement with any named executive, no golden parachute, no excise-tax gross-up, no defined-benefit pension, two clawback policies, hedging prohibited outright, pledging prohibited, repricing prohibited without shareholder approval, and ownership guidelines of 5x salary for the CEO. The soft spots are the combined Chair and CEO role, personal aircraft use permitted for Lobo alone at $474,033 of incremental cost in 2025, and Bain & Company — chaired by a director — as a paid consultant. Say-on-pay support has declined from the mid-90s to 87-92%.

Retention rests on very little. For performance stock units granted from 2024 onward, retirement at age 55 with ten years of service means continued vesting in full on the original schedule rather than pro rata, and vested options run to their original expiry. Lobo is 60, joined in 2011 and is retirement-eligible now. Insider ownership moves in two directions: Lobo's outright holding rose 4.1x since 2018 to 197,661 shares, about 9x his guideline, while Ronda Stryker's holding declined 9,282,027 shares, or 37.7%, in eight consecutive years without a single year of increase, taking officer-and-director ownership from 7.3% to 4.6%. No purpose is disclosed and no Form 4 record was available in the local stores.

Candor. Explicit error-acknowledgment language is close to absent across the 50 earnings transcripts in the record; almost every use of "admittedly" or "candidly" in twelve years qualifies a positive. The exception is unhedged and worth weighing: on spinal implants, Q4 2024, "we're not going to be investing in all the innovation on implants and having to deal with the management of the implant business, which, to be frank, we have not done a great job over the past 10, 12 years." Under the Q1 2026 cyber incident management declined to give any business-level sales detail, declined to confirm or decompose the impact when an analyst put $375m on the table, declined to discuss remediation learnings, and reaffirmed full-year guidance. Set against that, it volunteered the operational detail, stated on the Q2 2026 call that cyber costs run through adjusted EPS rather than around it, and narrowed rather than rebased the guide.

Acquisitions consumed 74.0% of operating cash flow and 92.2% of free cash flow. Dividends accounted for 30.2% and buybacks 2.8%. Total discretionary outflow of $38,559m against $30,436m of operating cash left an $8,123m gap, funded by $9,510m of net new debt. Incremental debt funded 42.2% of the M&A bill. Total debt went from $3,998m at end-2015 to $15,859m at end-2025 and goodwill from $4,136m to $19,291m; goodwill plus intangibles of $24,972m now exceeds book equity of $22,420m.

Per-share outcomes. Diluted shares rose 8.0m, or 2.1%, over the decade. Every per-share line grew roughly four to six percentage points less than its absolute counterpart: net sales per share +117.2% against +121.8% absolute, adjusted operating income per share +123.9% against +128.7%, free cash flow per share +194.2% against +200.6%, adjusted net earnings per share +135.0% against +140.1%. Share issuance is a small persistent leak rather than a driver.

The margin record on $22.5bn of M&A. Adjusted operating margin went 25.5% (2016), 26.3% (2019), 24.2% (2023), 25.3% (2024), 26.3% (2025) — roughly 80bps of expansion over nine years on revenue that grew 122%. Management met both targets it set: the 2023 Investor Day pledge to "get back to its 2019 op margin by 2025" was delivered at 26.29% against 26.25%, and the stated 200bps from the 2023 base was delivered as 210bps. Both are clean, verifiable deliveries. The same numbers also show it took six years to recover a margin the company already had in 2019.

Return on the capital deployed. Invested capital went from $12,848m (end-2016) to $34,268m (end-2025). On an adjusted basis, NOPAT went from $2,387m to $5,606m using each year's disclosed adjusted effective tax rate of 17.3% and 15.1%, so the incremental return on the $21,420m added is 15.0% [estimate]. On a GAAP basis, operating income taxed at each year's GAAP rate of 14.3% and 28.1% gives NOPAT of $1,864m to $3,515m and an incremental return of 7.7% [estimate]. Most of the gap is the purchased-intangible amortization and acquisition charges the adjusted measure excludes, but part of it is the tax rate: the two measures use different rates in both years, and FY2025's 28.1% GAAP rate is itself a one-year artefact. A buyer who treats acquired intangibles as a real economic cost gets the low number; one who treats them as sunk gets the high one.

Buybacks: when they happened, when they did not. The record is $850m over ten years, 3.5% of decade free cash flow. When Stryker bought, the timing was good — 2019's implied average of about $162 was 19% below the year's mean close of $198.49 — but the dollar amount was fixed at roughly $300m a year regardless of price. The suspension was a financing decision: "When we issued the EUR 2.4 billion of senior unsecured notes we also announced our intention to suspend our share repurchase program in 2020 and 2021" (FY2019 10-K), notes issued in December 2019 to fund Wright Medical. The programme then stayed off through the deepest drawdown of the decade, with the $1,033m authorisation untouched and available throughout while the stock traded below $160 on thirteen sessions between 2020-03-12 and 2020-04-03 at an average of $145.43. Deploying it at that average would have retired 7.1m shares, 1.9% of the company, worth $2,298m at the 2026-07-31 close [estimate: $1,033m / $145.43 = 7.10m shares x $323.49]. The counter-argument is real: elective procedures had stopped and the Wright cash call was pending. The point is that the decision was never framed as a price call in either direction.

Dividends. Paid per share went from $1.52 (2016) to $3.36 (2025), with growth decelerating from 11.8% in 2017 to 5.0% in 2025 and 4.8% in H1 2026. The deceleration preceded the Investor Day statement that "we expect that dividend growth to moderate a bit". Payout is undemanding at 25% of adjusted net earnings and 30% of free cash flow, and no restricted-payments covenant constrains it.

Free-cash-flow conversion sits at the bottom of the stated band. Conversion of adjusted net earnings by year: 65.0%, 39.0%, 73.3%, 49.1%, 98.7%, 78.8%, 57.0%, 77.1%, 74.2%, 81.3%. The decade cumulative is 70.9%, at the bottom edge of the 70-80% target, and four of ten years were below the floor. Inventory is the reason: days inventory outstanding ran 194-241 across the decade, because consigned implants at customer sites are the working-capital cost of the surgeon-preference model. Sections 1.2 and 17.2 state the metric never dropped below 197; that conflict is unresolved and is recorded in Section 19. Days payable outstanding expanded from 42 (2016) to 73-75 (2022-2025), which is what pulled the cash conversion cycle back from 254 days to 200.

H1 2026 is the first deleveraging half of the decade. Operating cash flow rose 35.3% to $1,842m and free cash flow 39.7% to $1,474m despite the cyber shutdown; acquisition spend was $459m against $4,814m; and $750m of net debt was repaid against $9,510m raised over 2016-2025. That combination is the condition the CFO cited when announcing the buyback resumption.

11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

Stryker is a disciplined serial acquirer with one large, clearly identified failure and one deal that is too young to grade but already showing strain. Cumulative goodwill impairment across 2013-2025 is $672m — $216m in 2022 and $456m in 2024 — and every dollar of it sits in one reporting unit, Spine; against a $19,291m goodwill balance that is 3.5%. Total goodwill and other impairments were larger and included long-lived asset write-offs: $170m (2025), $977m (2024) and $36m (2023). Twelve years of deals across 22 business units produced goodwill write-downs in exactly one of them. The largest deals built the current business: MAKO bought a loss-making company with declining revenue and became the anchor of a $9,469m segment; Wright Medical grew Trauma and Extremities from $1,639m (2019) to $3,948m (2025); Sage and Physio-Control sit inside a Medical business that went from $2,524m (2020) to $4,204m (2025).

What is not disciplined is the reporting. Stryker set two deal-level return standards and reported against neither, promised annual Vocera metrics and delivered them once qualitatively, and has never published a realized synergy dollar or a realized return for any of the roughly 60 deals management counts over the last decade.

Cash paid for acquisitions net of cash acquired totals $26,796m over 2013 to H1 2026; adding the assumed convertible notes redeemed as financing outflows — $1,440m for Wright and $425m for Vocera — the true outlay is about $28,661m.

The one failure, traced. K2M cost $1,380m in November 2018. The Spine reporting unit's fair value exceeded carrying amount by 10% at the October 2023 test and no charge was taken; fourteen months later it was impaired $273m, with a further $183m of goodwill allocated to the held-for-sale disposal group written off and a $362m valuation allowance to mark the group to fair value less cost to sell, plus roughly $33m more in H1 2025. Adding the 2022 charge of $216m gives about $1,067m of identified write-downs. That 10%-headroom-then-impairment sequence is the calibration to apply to the current Peripheral Vascular disclosure of 12% headroom on $3,203m.

The live risk. Inari's reporting unit was tested quantitatively eight months after closing and Stryker's own explanation is fair: a unit tested that close to acquisition will price near what was paid. Two facts sit against it. The precedent above. And the revenue is going the wrong way: Vascular quarterly net sales ran $406m (Q1 2025), $498m, $525m, $539m, $517m and then $496m in Q2 2026, the first fully organic comparison after Inari anniversaried in February 2026, at -1.8% constant currency and -6.7% in the United States. Normalizing for the disclosed supply drag gives roughly +5.6% to +8.6% constant currency [estimate: adding back 50-75bps of the Q2 2025 consolidated base of $6,022m, or $30-45m, to Vascular's $496m] — about half the rate that justified 8.1x forward sales, though the blend includes roughly $1.3bn of legacy neurovascular growing mid-single digits, so it is not a clean measure of Inari alone.

Synergy record. Wright: targets given, "exceeded expectations" asserted in Q4 2022, no dollar figure and no ROIC ever produced, and year five ended in 2025. Vocera: explicitly not a cost-synergy deal, with a promise on the Q1 2023 call to "provide some more metrics on that at the end of the year, and we plan to probably do that on an annual basis as we do with Mako" — delivered once as "pleased with the accelerating double-digit sales and order growth", then dropped, and Vocera has since been merged into Smart Care so a standalone measure is impossible even in principle. Sage and Physio: no standalone revenue or margin has ever been published. Inari, Cerus, Mobius, OrthoSpace, Gauss and every 2024 deal: no target to track. The cost of getting synergies is disclosed: acquisition-and-integration charges were $508m in 2025, $154m in 2024 and $20m in 2023, and amortization of purchased intangibles was $732m in 2025, 15.0% of GAAP operating income and permanently excluded from every guided figure.

Divestiture pricing is untestable. Neither the FTC-mandated ankle and finger-joint sale to DJO nor the April 2025 US spinal implants sale to Viscogliosi Brothers has a disclosed consideration from either side, so the round-trip multiple on K2M cannot be computed. The only quantitative handle is the 10-K's statement that consideration for the spine sale could increase by up to $57m or decrease by up to $245m.

Two things about deal terms have changed. Contingent consideration has become routine — up to $110m on OrthoSpace, $130m on Mobius, $40m on Gauss, $225m on Cerus, $400m across the 2024 deals and $400m on Amplitude Vascular — and Stryker discloses fair-value changes only inside the acquisition-and-integration line, never per deal, so no earn-out has a verifiable pass or fail. And the two most recent large deals are the first where Stryker bought unprofitable and pre-revenue assets: Inari at 8.1x forward revenue on decelerating growth with an open Anti-Kickback civil investigative demand outstanding at signing, and Amplitude Vascular at $706m with no revenue, no approval and a purchase-price allocation of nothing but in-process R&D and goodwill.

12. Capitalization and balance sheet

Stryker funds itself with one instrument type: fixed-rate senior unsecured notes issued by the parent. At 2026-06-30 there were 20 tranches outstanding totalling $14,691m of carrying value, plus $250m of commercial paper and $1m of other borrowings, for $14,942m of gross debt. No secured debt, no term loans, no convertibles, no preferred stock, no material pension deficit and no floating-rate exposure other than the commercial paper. The $3,000m revolver maturing 2030-02-25 is undrawn.

Weighted-average cost of debt. Principal-weighted stated coupon across the stack, since there are no floating legs other than commercial paper and no converts. Cash interest rate computed as annualized interest expense on debt and credit facilities divided by average gross debt.

The principal-weighted coupon was 3.473% at 2026-06-30 (3.462% at 2025-12-31): 4.180% on $9,075m of USD notes, 61.8% of the stack, and 2.331% on $5,616m of EUR notes, 38.2%. Including commercial paper at roughly 4.4% takes it to 3.489%. The all-in cash rate is higher because of fees and discount amortization: Q2 2026 interest expense on debt and credit facilities of $136m annualizes to $544m against average gross debt of $14,833m, an all-in 3.67%. FY2025's income-statement interest expense of $607m and Note 10's $582m of interest on debt and facilities differ by design: Note 11 states that interest on uncertain tax positions is included in interest expense, so $582m is the figure for cost-of-debt work and $607m for coverage.

The maturity wall is the real cost. Face-value repayments are $1,000m in 2026 (paid in March), $3,988m in 2027-2028, $4,256m in 2029-2030 and $6,729m after 2030, so $8,244m of face, 56% of the remaining stack, matures in the four years 2027-2030 at a 3.24% carrying-value-weighted coupon. Stryker's own most recent primary prints are the February 2025 issuance at 4.550% for two years through 5.200% for ten, a blended 4.9% on $3,000m. Refinancing the wall at a flat 4.5% adds $102m a year and at 4.9% adds $134m [estimate: $8,112m of carrying value at 4.5-4.9% against a 3.24% embedded coupon; the range is wide because a majority of the wall is euro-denominated and would refinance on the euro curve]. Against FY2025 pre-tax income of $4,514m that is 2.3-3.0%. The sharpest single block is the sub-2.5% tranche: $3,610m at Jun-2026, 24.2% of gross debt, at a 1.46% weighted coupon. The market already prices this: the notes are marked at $14,024m against $14,691m of carrying value, a 4.5% discount to par. The H1 2026 decline in interest expense, from $296m to $278m, is a one-off from retiring $1,000m of 3.500% notes with balance-sheet cash rather than refinancing, and does not extend.

Covenants. The 10-Ks disclose only that Stryker "was in compliance with all covenants". The February 2025 credit agreement, filed as an exhibit to an 8-K, sets a single financial covenant: Leverage Ratio, defined as gross Consolidated Funded Indebtedness over trailing four-quarter Consolidated EBITDA with no cash netting, may not exceed 3.75:1.00. Consolidated EBITDA is generous, admitting non-cash charges, deal fees and projected cost savings and synergies on a pro-forma basis. Twice during the term, in connection with an acquisition above $750m of consideration, the cap steps to 4.75x for four quarters and then declines through 4.50x, 4.25x and 4.00x. There is no interest-coverage covenant and no restricted-payments covenant, so nothing contractually limits dividends or buybacks. On GAAP EBITDA, which understates covenant EBITDA, gross debt of $14,942m against LTM EBITDA of $6,755m is 2.21x against a 3.75x cap — 1.54 turns of headroom, or $10.4bn of incremental debt at flat EBITDA, and $17.1bn under an acquisition holiday. EBITDA would have to decline 41% at flat debt before a breach.

The covenant history shows the one episode where it plausibly bound: the August 2016 agreement set 3.5:1; on 2020-04-30 Stryker raised it to 4.5:1 through mid-2021 and then exercised the acquisition clause to 5.0:1 effective 2020-12-31, when gross leverage reached 4.61x on the Wright Medical close into a COVID-depressed EBITDA base. The October 2021 and February 2025 agreements settled at 3.75.

Deleveraging happened through EBITDA growth rather than repayment: gross debt at YE2025 was 13% higher than at YE2020 while net leverage halved. The Inari deal did not repeat 2020 — $4,960m of FY2025 acquisition spend funded with $2,979m of new notes and cash, gross debt up $2,262m, and net leverage unchanged at 1.9x because FY2025 EBITDA grew 28%. LTM leverage through Q2 2026 is 1.70x net and 2.21x gross, an improvement in one half driven by the March 2026 repayment and the H1 EBITDA step-up. Interest coverage troughed at 8.1x in FY2025 while the Inari financing was outstanding for eleven months, and has recovered to 9.2x. Bloomberg reports net debt/EBITDA of 1.55x and gross of 2.05x for the same date; its own EBITDA field of $6,287m is not the denominator implied by those ratios, and its debt figure of $16,360m includes $501m of capitalized operating leases. The filing-derived figures are used throughout.

Ratings are split one notch: Moody's A3 stable, upgraded from Baa1 on 2025-06-18, and S&P BBB+ stable, affirmed 2025-04-25 (Bloomberg, pulled 2026-07-31; corroborated at investing.com and cbonds.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web]. The credit agreement's Applicable Margin runs off the higher of the two on a split rating, so the Moody's upgrade moved the facility from Pricing Level 3 (0.090% facility fee, 0.910% drawn) to Level 2 (0.080%, 0.795%). On an undrawn facility that saves about $0.3m a year; its value is as confirmation of the rating trajectory. No Stryker filing names an agency or a rating — the FY2025 10-K says only that it continues to have "strong investment-grade short-term and long-term debt ratings".

Leases and pension are immaterial. Operating leases only: right-of-use assets $519m, lease liabilities $501m, weighted-average remaining term 5.0 years at a 3.77% discount rate. Capitalizing them moves gross leverage from 2.21x to 2.29x. Non-US defined-benefit plans are underfunded by $269m against $22,420m of equity, with $23m of employer contributions in 2025 and $24m expected in 2026.

Share-based compensation and dilution. Buybacks stopped after 2019 and did not resume for six and a half years, so cumulative 2016-2025 SBC of $1,614m against $850m of repurchases went straight into the share count. Net dilution is nonetheless small: shares outstanding went from 374.5m at YE2019 to 382.5m at YE2025, +0.35% a year, and +0.25% a year across the full decade. SBC was 0.97% of FY2025 revenue and 4.8% of operating cash flow. Gross issuance is shrinking — 2.0m shares in 2019 to 1.1m in 2025 — because Stryker settles a growing share of vesting in cash withholding rather than issuing gross shares, which converts dilution into cash outflow: $149m, $195m and $155m of cash paid for taxes on withheld shares in 2025, 2024 and 2023, and $146m in H1 2026 alone. Options outstanding at YE2025 were 10.4m, 2.7% of shares, at a weighted exercise price of $234.56.

The diluted count is temporarily flattered by the share price. The dilutive effect of employee stock compensation declined to 2.5m shares in Q2 2026 from 4.2m in Q2 2025, pulling diluted shares to 386.0m from 386.4m even though basic shares rose from 382.2m to 383.5m, because SYK at $323.49 sits nearer the $234.56 weighted-average strike. That is worth about a cent of quarterly EPS. It is not an improvement in the equity-compensation burden, because SBC rose to $141m in H1 2026 from $133m, and it reverses mechanically if the stock recovers.

Structural risks, ranked by expected loss rather than tail severity.

  1. Refinancing the 2027-2030 wall: certain to happen, $102-134m a year by 2030, already visible in the mark-to-market.
  2. Translation on the euro debt block: EUR 5.0bn is designated as a net investment hedge so the effect goes to other comprehensive income rather than earnings, and the after-tax loss recognised there on designated net investment hedges was $715m in 2025, 3.2% of shareholders' equity in one year, reversing when the euro weakens.
  3. The German assessment of $754m plus $11m expected, the only contingent cash claim large enough to matter, against $403m of total unrecognized tax benefits that Stryker did not increase after receiving it.
  4. Covenant proximity, which is negligible.
  5. Floating-rate exposure of $250m, 1.7% of gross debt; Item 7A discloses no interest-rate sensitivity at all.
  6. Structural subordination, contractually capped at 20% of consolidated net worth (about $4.5bn on the $22,420m of equity at 2026-06-30) and effectively nil today.
  7. Pension, which is not a risk.

One constraint applies to the buyback. Cash held outside the United States moved from 20% at 2025-12-31 to 51% at 2026-06-30, so US cash declined from roughly $3,280m to roughly $1,703m while offshore cash rose from roughly $820m to roughly $1,773m [estimate: applying the disclosed percentages to the disclosed totals]. The $1,033m authorisation would absorb about 60% of the remaining domestic balance. Stryker can fund domestically with commercial paper, and drew $250m in Q2 2026 for the first time since 2018, so this is a sequencing point rather than a blocker, and it is why the CFO hedged on size and made the buyback contingent on deal flow.

13.4 What actually drove the decade

Revenue grew 122% over 2016-2025 and adjusted operating margin expanded roughly 80bps. Gross margin declined 350bps from 66.3% (2016) to 62.8% (2022) and recovered 120bps to 64.0% (2025) without regaining the pre-2020 level, and management says it will not: segment mix runs the wrong way because the lower-gross-margin segment grows faster.▪ The two drivers of the 2016-2022 decline were mix and price, compounding at -0.7% to -1.4% a year. The 2024-to-2025 bridge is the cleanest single view: +40bps and +10bps from sales pricing and +60bps and +70bps from volume and mix were almost entirely consumed by 60bps of purchase-accounting inventory step-up from Inari, so underlying gross margin improved while reported gross margin moved 10bps.

Returns tell the other half. On a normalized 15% tax basis ROIC was 19.9% in 2015 and 13.0% in 2025 — after the two strongest operating years in the company's history, seven points below where it started. The cause is arithmetic: invested capital grew $25,749m over the decade against cumulative acquisition spend of $22,518m, 87% of the build, while operating income grew $3,017m and goodwill rose from $4,136m to $19,291m. ROIC excluding goodwill and intangibles stayed in a 30-40% band throughout. Rolling three-year incremental returns on a normalized tax basis locate the damage precisely: 14.8%, 13.0%, 6.0%, 7.2%, (0.7)%, 0.6%, 1.3% for the windows ending 2016 through 2022, then 31.6%, 17.4% and 27.0% for 2023-2025. Incremental returns on capital deployed between 2015 and 2022 were at or below the cost of capital for seven consecutive windows; the three most recent windows measure incremental NOPAT against a base depressed by COVID and by those same low-return acquisitions, and Inari at $4,810m is too recent to appear.

One discontinued metric deserves its own line. Spinal Implants revenue ran $713m (2023), $707m (2024), $185m (2025) and $3m in Q2 2026 after the April 2025 divestiture, and is the whole of the apparent Orthopaedics slowdown: the segment grew 10.9% ex-spine in 2025 against 4.3% as reported.▪ One new metric has a short history: Ortho Tech, created in Q1 2026, grew 10.0% constant currency in Q2 2026 with US +9.5% and International +11.8%.

The KPI set has a structural weakness. Stryker discloses no units, no ASPs, no procedure counts, no attach rates, no renewal rates, no per-system Mako utilization (the disclosed figure is the share of Stryker's own procedures done on Mako, a mix statistic), and no order book. The only operating quantity disclosed as a series is organic growth and its price/volume split.

That is the whole internal-versus-external gap: the Street takes management's word on margin, EPS and cash conversion to the decimal, and takes the revenue line at the bottom.

The record behind the guidance. Stryker beat the top of its initial full-year organic guide in nine of the ten comparable years by a median of about 125bps, and beat the top of its initial adjusted-EPS range in eight of ten by a mean of 1.56%. The conservatism is asymmetric and management explains it: "If we start moving the top line up, we're not going to just reinvest all of it. There will be an amount that we drop through" (Q4 2025 call). Realised flow-through of the top-line beat into the EPS beat has declined in each of the last three years, from about 1.6x (2023) to 1.5x (2024) to 1.3x (2025), so modelling a top-line beat at more than about 1.3x into EPS is not supported by the recent record. Two failures matter: 2020, when guidance was withdrawn, and 2022, when organic growth beat the top of the guide by 170bps and adjusted EPS still came in $0.26 below the bottom of the January range on foreign exchange and supply-chain inflation.

FY2026 breaks the revision pattern. In each of 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 management raised the organic guide by the half. In 2026 it held at Q1 and then narrowed at Q2, raising the floor 30bps and cutting the ceiling 20bps, the first downward move in any part of the organic range since Q3 2021. The adjusted-EPS range for FY2026 is $0.15 wide after the Q2 narrowing to $14.95-$15.10, 1.0% of the midpoint and the narrowest in twelve years, against an organic range 50bps wider than 2025's. The earnings number is the commitment and the sales number is the variable.

What is no longer guided. Quarterly EPS guidance was withdrawn in January 2021 and has not returned. The explicit annual adjusted-operating-margin target, given every January through 2025, was not given for FY2026; asked directly, the CFO said "I think if you plug that in, you'll see it's a healthy margin that we're planning for '26". Capital-expenditure guidance, $800-850m for FY2025, was also dropped. The company-level "200-300bps above market" was replaced by "high end of med tech" with an explicit refusal to number it: "we don't know what the procedure growth is going to be over the next 3 years… If the market conditions change, we're not going to defy gravity."

Where the base rates bite hardest. Consensus's 8.5% revenue CAGR for 2025-2028 sits at roughly the 90th percentile of the realised medtech distribution above $20bn of revenue, where the median outcome was 1.3%.▪ No pure medical-device company in the reference class has compounded revenue at 8%-plus for five years from a base above $20bn without a transformational acquisition; all five instances are Abbott windows spanning a goodwill step from $7,683m to $24,020m. Two facts cut the other way and belong beside it. Stryker has not decayed with scale — its trailing three-year reported CAGR was 10.8% at $25bn in 2025 against 7.2% at $9bn in 2013 — and among the 34 company-years in the class that compounded 8%-plus from above $10bn, the median added $1.14 of goodwill per $1 of revenue while Stryker's 2020-2025 window added $0.61, the fourth-cheapest of the 34.

Q4 adjusted EPS beat 6.0% on revenue 3.8% above consensus, and the FY2024 guide was set above the prevailing consensus: organic growth of 7.5-9.0% and adjusted EPS of $11.70-$12.00 against a FY2024 consensus of $11.56 eight days earlier, which moved to $11.83 within two sessions. The CEO also introduced an accelerated margin-expansion plan on the same call.
2026:Q1 (6.5)% The only EPS miss in the twelve quarters and a large one: $2.60 against $2.985 consensus and revenue $315m light. Cause disclosed on the call: a cyber incident late in the quarter wiped approximately 40,000 laptops and halted global manufacturing for almost three weeks, with production fully restored the week of 1 April. Organic growth 2.4%, adjusted operating margin 21.1%. Full-year guidance was maintained and management declined to give business-level detail.
2026:Q2 (7.1)% A 6.1% EPS beat and a 7.1% decline. Four disclosed items: the beat was attributed partly to "the tariff refunds that are happening that happened in the quarter" with offsetting cyber costs landing in H2; the beat did not flow through, with FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance moving only from $14.90-$15.10 to $14.95-$15.10 after a $0.21 quarterly beat, which the first analyst question put to management directly; the organic sales guide had its top end cut from 9.5% to 9.3%; and revenue met consensus without exceeding it while US Vascular organic sales declined 6.7% on a peripheral-vascular supply disruption that produced "a meaningful back order situation with lost sales in the quarter". Contemporaneous reporting attributes the move to the same combination (markets.financialcontent.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web].

Across the 42 quarters from 2016:Q1 to 2026:Q2, Stryker beat consensus adjusted EPS in 34 (81%) with a median surprise of +1.8% and a mean of +3.2%, the mean pulled up by 2020:Q3. The reaction distribution does not follow: the median next-session reaction was (0.9)%, the mean (0.16)%, and 26 of 42 sessions (62%) were negative. Beating consensus by one or two percent has been the expected outcome rather than new information. The most recent six prints averaged (2.6)% against +0.4% for the preceding eight, so the pattern has sharpened.

15.4 The decade's major moves

Rank Peak Trough Peak-to-trough What changed
1 2020-02-19, $225.10 2020-03-23, $126.50 (43.8)% Elective procedures suspended. Guidance withdrawn — the only withdrawal in the 2014-2026 record. FY2020 sales declined 3.6% reported and 4.8% organic, the only revenue decline of the decade. Three of the decade's five worst sessions sit inside the window, and the worst single session, (13.1)% on 2020-04-01, came nine sessions after the trough.
2 2021-09-08, $280.09 2022-07-18, $189.27 (32.4)% Earnings and multiple together. Twelve-month-forward consensus EPS was $10.17 at end-2021 and $9.82 at end-2022, a decline. The disclosed cause was the electronic-component and supply-chain crisis; management held guidance in Q1 2022 rather than cutting, and took a $216m Spine goodwill impairment that year.
3 2025-07-25, $403.53 2026-05-11, $282.58 (30.0)% The current drawdown and a multiple event rather than an earnings event. Sequence: three negative post-print sessions on in-line quarters, the 11 March 2026 cyber incident (SYK closed at $345.78 that day, (3.6)%, after (2.0)% on 10 March and a further (2.5)% on 12 March), the Q1 2026 print at (6.5)%, then a further slide to the May trough.
4 2018-06-06, $179.78 2018-12-24, $145.00 (19.3)% Broad Q4-2018 market drawdown; the forward multiple moved from 22x to 20x while forward EPS rose 12%. The subsequent print produced the decade's third-best session, +11.4% on 2019-01-30.
5 2023-06-30, $305.09 2023-10-12, $253.85 (16.8)% The GLP-1 de-rating. Investors sold orthopaedic exposure on the thesis that weight-loss drugs would reduce joint-replacement demand, with "many investors anticipating negative action and selling off stocks rather than waiting to see how the new drugs would affect earnings reports" (massdevice.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web]. Stryker's reported numbers did not deteriorate: FY2023 organic growth was 11.5% and adjusted EPS $10.60 against $9.34.

Dispersion is unusually tight. The FY2026 high-to-low spread across 27 estimates is $0.41, 2.7% of the mean, and the range straddles management's own $14.95-$15.10 guidance issued the day before, reaching $0.21 below the floor and $0.05 above the ceiling; the mean is $0.03 below the guidance midpoint. FY2029 has nine contributors, which is why its band is wider. On a GAAP basis consensus is $12.95, $15.15 and $17.12 for FY2026-FY2028, implying 25x, 21x and 19x, with the adjusted-to-GAAP gap narrowing from 14% to 8% of adjusted EPS — the same gap measured against GAAP EPS, the basis Sections 14 and 17.4 use, runs from 62.3% in FY2025 to 9.0% in FY2028 — and no published bridge explaining the composition of that narrowing.

Broker positioning as of 2026-07-31, reported as the sources' views and not adopted: 30 covering analysts, 26 buy-equivalent, 4 hold, 0 sell, consensus rating 4.7 of 5, mean target price $384.85 and median $380 against the $323.49 price. Published targets span $315 (Pito Chickering, Deutsche Bank, dated 2026-05-01) to $465 (Choong-Hyun Kim, Mirae Asset, 2026-05-04); the lowest target among analysts who updated after the Q2 print is $316 (Debbie Wang, Morningstar, 2026-07-31). Eleven of the targets are dated 2026-07-30 or 2026-07-31. The distribution has no bear: the most negative published view is that the stock is worth roughly what it already trades for. Two positions inside the bull camp function as de facto scepticism: JPMorgan at overweight with a $350 target, the lowest of any bulge-bracket buyer, and Evercore at outperform with $355.

The disagreement is not about the earnings. The FY2027 consensus EPS spread across 27 estimates is 3.7% and the revenue spread across 25 is 2.6%; the target-price spread across 26 published targets is 47.6%.

17. Forward model summary

The model projects FY2026-FY2033 from ten business lines, each on its own organic constant-currency growth driver, with foreign exchange and the spinal-implants run-off added at the top. It is an operating model only: it runs from revenue to free cash flow and contains no valuation, no multiple and no discount rate. It is built on the FY2025 10-K reportable-segment basis, so its segment lines will not match 2026 and later 10-Q segment totals; a memo line converts each forecast year onto the reported basis using an estimated $1,890m FY2025 net transfer [estimate: Orthopaedic Instruments in at about $2,020m less spine Enabling Technologies out at about $130m].
