17.2 Assumptions

Driver Bear Base Bull Provenance Challenge
H2 2026 organic growth 7.9% 10.9% 13.4% mgmt-guidance Holds. The bear is more severe than its own description: H1 at 5.8% plus H2 at the clean Q2 rate gives 7.5% for the year, not 6.9%
Instruments growth, 2026-33 avg 3.6% 6.1% 8.6% historical-record Holds. Below the 8.3% compounded over 2017-2025, and the fade is to a stated 4-5 year launch cadence rather than to an average
Endoscopy growth, 2026-33 avg 4.1% 6.6% 9.1% historical-record Weak. The stated reason — the 1888 replacement has no date, so the cycle fades before it renews — is contradicted by a platform that has renewed roughly every four years since 2004. The line compounded 9.0% over 2019-2025 and printed +11.7% in Q2 2026. A 7.0-7.5% base with the current path as bear is better supported
Medical growth, 2026-33 avg 4.3% 6.8% 9.3% historical-record Holds. The line compounded 10.9% over 2019-2025, but the largest identified driver is a one-time fleet swap, and the recurring offset is bounded by a contract-liability balance that declined in H1 2026
Vascular growth, 2026-33 avg 3.4% 9.1% 12.3% analyst-judgment Weak. The line has never grown near 9% organically in any disclosed year: legacy neurovascular compounded 3.2% over 2021-2024, FY2025's +50.6% was the Inari consolidation, and Q2 2026 was -1.8% constant currency. The 11-13% assumed for 2027-2029 assigns the base case to the favourable branch of a binary trial readout. The range is honestly wide and the modeller flags it as the largest single judgment, but the base should be understood as probability-weighted
Neuro Cranial growth, 2026-33 avg 4.6% 7.1% 9.6% historical-record Weak. The stated justification is factually wrong: the interventional-spine reclassification was made in 2024 and applied to every year in the table, so it cannot inflate one year's growth. Reported growth of 13.9% (2024) and 16.3% (2025) is substantially organic, so a 7.1% base is a large haircut supported by a mechanism that does not exist. A different fact supports the direction — the restated Instruments line containing Neuro Cranial grew only 9.3% in Q2 2026 — and the base should be re-anchored on that, nearer 8%
Knees growth, 2026-33 avg 3.4% 5.4% 7.1% historical-record Holds. The line compounded 6.5-6.6% through the entire Mako scaling, US penetration above two-thirds caps the remaining mix benefit, and the CY2027 fee proposal and GLP-1 evidence are unmodelled
Hips growth, 2026-33 avg 3.0% 4.8% 6.5% historical-record Weak. The path assumes a 200bp recovery in 2027-2028 off a deceleration nobody has explained: international hips went from +11.2% constant currency in FY2025 to -0.6% in H1 2026 with zero dollar growth in Q2, and no filing or call gives a reason. Flatten to 4.0-4.5% or move the recovery into the bull
Trauma and Extremities growth, 2026-33 avg 6.5% 8.7% 10.5% historical-record Holds. The 2022-2025 window is post-Wright, clean of material acquisitions and compounded 12.0%; the exposure is the most robust in the model; the 7.0% terminal equals market growth with zero outgrowth
Other Orthopaedics growth, 2026-33 avg 4.8% 7.3% 9.8% historical-record Holds. Compounded 10.4% over 2022-2025, and Ortho Tech grew 10.0% constant currency in Q2 2026
Price contribution (0.25)%/yr 0.0%/yr +0.5%/yr historical-record Weak on the bear. Price was negative in every year 2014-2022, averaging about -1.2pp, and Stryker guided "unfavorable price reductions of 1.5% to 2%" for both 2016 and 2017. A -1.0% to -1.5% bear is the historically supported tail, and at close to full flow-through that is worth roughly 250-375bps of consolidated operating margin over eight years — enough to erase both segments' assumed margin expansion
FX, FY2026 +0.7% +0.7% +0.7% mgmt-guidance Weak. The point estimate is well anchored on the disclosed Q1 +1.6% and Q2 +0.4%, but the zero-width range deletes a variable whose disclosed annual contribution ranged from -4.2% to +1.1% over 2014-2025. Widen to roughly +0.4% to +1.0%
MedSurg segment margin, FY2033 30.1% 31.3% 33.2% historical-record Holds. 17.5bps a year is below the segment's own realised 20bps a year over 2020-2025, and rests on an identified mix mechanism — Vascular at an 85-88% gross margin growing fastest — rather than on a leverage claim
Orthopaedics segment margin, FY2033 30.7% 32.1% 33.8% historical-record Weak. Needs ~29bps a year for eight consecutive years from a segment whose underlying margin was flat to down in FY2025 once the divestiture is removed, and it is not independent of the price assumption: an eight-year reversion to the 2014-2022 price regime is worth roughly 390-780bps of segment margin, three or more times the assumed expansion
Corporate and Other, % of revenue 3.68% 3.32% 3.00% historical-record Holds. FY2025 already reversed a third of the prior drift unaided, and the bear sits above the FY2025 actual
Adjusted operating margin, FY2028 26.2% 27.4% 28.5% analyst-judgment Holds. 42bps below management's stated floor and 34bps below consensus, against a class median of -0.1pp over three years, with the gap explained by dated items: the tariff reversal does not repeat, remediation lands in H2, and the ~$400m FY2026 tariff assumption is stale
Amortization of acquired intangibles, FY2026 $740m $740m $740m historical-record Weak. H1 2026 was $355m against $354m a year earlier, so doubling gives $710m and the Amplitude close adds perhaps $10-20m; $715-730m is the supported range. The zero-width band also contradicts the assumption's own justification that every acquisition stops this line falling
Non-amortization special charges, FY2026 $780m $700m $620m analyst-judgment Weak. H1 2026 actuals total $286m, annualising to $572m, below the bull case. Reaching $700m requires H2 charges 45% above H1. The cyber-remediation and integration spend management guided to H2 makes it defensible as a prudence buffer, but it is a buffer rather than an estimate
Interest expense, FY2033 $850m $730m $615m historical-record Weak. The refinancing arithmetic is sound but not internally consistent with zero acquisitions: on the model's own cash figures a true zero-M&A Stryker extinguishes net debt by roughly 2029-30 and retires the wall rather than refinancing it. The honest statement is that $730m is the interest expense conditional on the M&A programme continuing, in which case the revenue line is too low
Interest and other income, FY2026 $162.5m $170m $177.5m analyst-judgment Weak. Back-solved so that net other expense of about $415m matches the ~$420m the CFO named, so it inherits any error in the interest assumption. The line ran $148m, $212m and $232m over 2023-2025; a ±$7.5m band is far narrower than its own variability
Adjusted effective tax rate 16.5% 15.5% 15.0% mgmt-guidance Holds. Q1 2026 was 14.5% and Q2 16.5%, weighting to about 15.5% for the half, and the bear covers Pillar Two creep and the German assessment
Capital expenditure, FY2026 $845.6m $830.6m $826.8m historical-record Refuted. H1 2026 capex was $368m, up 20.3%, and Stryker's capex is H1-light: 42.3% of the year in 2024 and 40.2% in 2025. Applying the mean split gives about $890m for FY2026, with an $870-915m band. Every scenario sits below it, and the cyber laptop replacement and an in-flight ERP implementation both add H2 capex. The miss is one-sided and worth roughly $60m of free cash flow
Capex, % of revenue thereafter 3.15% 3.01% 2.86% historical-record Weak. FY2026 alone breaks it at about 3.27%. Beyond 2026 a flat 3.0% is defensible against 2023-2025, but capex ran 4.2-4.8% of revenue over 2016-2019, capex has averaged 1.7x depreciation across the decade, and a large share of what Stryker calls capex is Mako systems and instrument sets placed with customers. Recentre 2026-2027 at about 3.2%
Core working capital, % of revenue 31.5% 29.5% 27.8% historical-record Weak. Every source of the 2023-2025 improvement is exhausted: days payable plateaued at 73-75, days sales outstanding hit a thirteen-year low of 59, and days inventory has never been below 197 because consigned implants are the working-capital cost of the model. Hold the ratio flat at 30.1% instead; the magnitude is roughly $386m of cumulative cash
FCF / adjusted net earnings, FY2033 83.4% 85.5% 87.2% historical-record Weak. The entire range sits above management's 70-80% target and at or above the top of the 72-84% base-rate band. The only year above 85% in the thirteen-year record is 2020. The stated mechanism double-counts with the working-capital assumption. Recentre at 78-83%
Diluted shares, FY2033 395.1m 384.0m 369.9m analyst-judgment Weak. The base extrapolates a policy one day old at the run date. The remaining authorisation of $1,033m is 0.83% of shares and about three years of gross issuance, yet the model's cash flow assumes $4,783m of cumulative repurchases over 2026-2033, 4.6x the authorised amount. The bear is simply the 2020-2025 revealed behaviour and is better supported
Dividend per share growth +4.0% +5.0% +6.0% mgmt-guidance Weak. Matches the current run-rate, but pairing 5.0% dividend growth with 6.7-10.6% adjusted EPS growth moves the payout ratio from 23.6% in 2026 to 19.3% by 2033, breaking a decade of stability at about 25% with no stated mechanism. Consensus disagrees: FY2029 DPS of $4.94 is roughly 15% above the model's implied path
Acquisition contribution to revenue 0.0% 0.0% 0.0% analyst-judgment Refuted as a statement about what will happen. Stryker's own MD&A gives the acquisition and divestiture contribution every year — 2.5, 0.9, 7.9, 2.7, 1.9, 2.6, 1.2, 5.5, 1.3, 0.1, 0.5, 0.4 percentage points for 2014-2025 — and it has never been zero in twelve years, with a median of about 1.6pp. At that median, eight years is worth roughly 13.5% of revenue, about $5.8bn on the FY2033 base. The convention is defensible — no unannounced deal can be modelled without inventing it, and consensus makes the same exclusion — but it is a convention rather than a forecast
Consolidated organic growth, FY2027-33 avg 3.8% 6.7% 8.9% base-rate Weak. The model's own reference class puts the 2027-2031 five-year average of about 7.1% at roughly the 85th-90th percentile: in 49 medtech company-years starting above $20bn since 2005 the median forward five-year CAGR was 1.3% and only 10% reached 8%. No pure device company in the class has compounded 8%-plus for five years from above $20bn without a transformational acquisition, and this model sets acquisition contribution to zero. The bear at 3.8% still sits above the class median, so no scenario reflects the modal outcome

17.3 Sensitivities

Each driver is moved one at a time from the base by a plausible amount; the figures are half the spread between the up and down runs, so each is the swing for a one-sided move. Base terminal year 2033: revenue $42,892m, adjusted operating income $12,180m, adjusted EPS $25.74, free cash flow $8,448m; cumulative 2026-2033 free cash flow $52,207m.

Rank Driver Move Change in 2033 adj. operating income as % Change in 2033 FCF Change in cumulative FCF Change in 2033 adj. EPS
1 Segment operating margin cadence, both segments ±20bps a year (±160bps by 2033) ±686 ±5.6% ±580 ±2,291 ±$1.51
2 MedSurg capital lines (Instruments, Endoscopy, Medical) ±150bps a year ±591 ±4.9% ±358 ±1,187 ±$1.30
3 Vascular growth (the PEERLESS II outcome) ±500bps a year ±415 ±3.4% ±241 ±756 ±$0.91
4 Trauma and Extremities growth ±200bps a year ±330 ±2.7% ±197 ±629 ±$0.73
5 Knees and Hips growth ±150bps a year ±224 ±1.8% ±138 ±466 ±$0.49
6 Corporate and Other, % of revenue ±30bps ±129 ±1.1% ±109 ±711 ±$0.28
7 Capital expenditure intensity ±40bps of revenue 0 — ±172 ±1,122 0
8 Adjusted effective tax rate ±100bps 0 — ±117 ±742 ±$0.30
9 Core working capital intensity ±150bps of revenue 0 — ±35 ±643 0

Three things follow from the ranking. The margin cadence outranks every revenue driver: a 20bp-a-year difference in segment margin expansion moves more terminal operating income than a 150bp-a-year difference in the growth rate of 45% of the revenue base, because Stryker's margin base is large and incremental margins are only 33-38%, so a point of margin is worth roughly three points of revenue. Mako is the smallest of the five revenue drivers — Knees and Hips are 18% of revenue, compounded 5.9% over 2019-2025 while the robot scaled from under 900 systems to over 3,000, and a 150bp-a-year change moves 2033 operating income by 1.8%. And working capital is invisible in the terminal year and large in aggregate, because a level shift in the stock is a one-time flow: a 150bp shift changes 2033 free cash flow by $35m and cumulative free cash flow by $643m.

17.4 Where the base case sits against consensus, and what it leaves out

FY2026 FY2027 FY2028 FY2029
Consensus revenue ($m) 27,282 29,612 32,040 34,583
Model base revenue ($m) 27,233 29,487 31,776 33,995
Difference (0.2)% (0.4)% (0.8)% (1.7)%
Consensus adjusted EPS ($) 15.00 16.75 18.66 20.65
Model base adjusted EPS ($) 15.02 16.61 18.10 19.60
Difference +0.2% (0.8)% (3.0)% (5.1)%
Consensus FCF ($m) 4,433 5,456 6,188 7,032
Model base FCF ($m) 4,575 5,168 5,710 6,254
Difference +3.2% (5.3)% (7.7)% (11.1)%

The base agrees with consensus on FY2026 to within 0.2% on both revenue and EPS and diverges progressively from FY2027, mostly on margin rather than revenue: the model expands adjusted operating margin at roughly 30bps a year against consensus's roughly 50bps.

Setting acquisitions to zero is not neutral. The base case generates $52,207m of cumulative free cash flow over 2026-2033, of which $12,969m goes to dividends and $4,783m to buybacks, leaving $34,455m of discretionary cash. At management's stated allocation of roughly 70% to M&A, that is about $24,100m of acquisition capacity, more than the entire FY2016-FY2025 programme of $22,518m, and it appears in no revenue line here or in consensus. At Inari's revenue multiple of roughly 8.0x that capacity buys about $3,000m of revenue; at Wright Medical's roughly 5.9x, about $4,100m — either way roughly 7-10% of the base-case FY2033 revenue line [estimate: capacity divided by the two disclosed deal multiples]. One qualification goes with that: Stryker's incremental return on invested capital by five-year window was 1.9% (2010-2015), 1.8% (2015-2020) and 20.7% (2020-2025), and the 2015-2020 window converted $16,055m of incremental invested capital into $286m of incremental NOPAT. If the next eight years resemble 2015-2020 rather than 2020-2025, that capital buys revenue and almost no earnings. Consensus's adjusted-to-GAAP EPS gap, measured against GAAP EPS, collapsing from +62.3% in FY2025 to +9.0% by FY2028 is the same exclusion visible from the other side: it implies essentially no new acquisition amortization, inventory step-up or integration charge. Both this model and consensus are wrong in the same direction if Stryker keeps buying.

The base case sits at roughly the 75th-80th percentile of the appropriate reference class on growth and around the 45th percentile on margin expansion.▪ It is a case in which Stryker keeps outgrowing the class but stops accelerating, and in which the margin commitment is missed by 42bps. It is not a pessimistic case, and the assumption review flags seventeen drivers as weak and two as refuted. Most of them, and both refutations, point in the direction of the base being too favourable.

18. Risks

1. Cyber recurrence and the unfinished tail of the March 2026 attack — high. On 11 March 2026 Stryker identified a destructive attack on its Microsoft environment. The Q1 2026 10-Q states it "resulted in a disruption to our corporate network environment and caused disruption to our business operations", and an 8-K/A dated 9 April 2026 under Item 1.05 determined the incident "had a material impact on our operations". Manufacturing was down until the week of 1 April, roughly three weeks. Press reporting attributes it to Handala, a group Check Point Research identified and which Palo Alto Networks researchers have linked to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security, executed by abusing the device-management platform to issue mass remote-wipe commands rather than by ransomware (medtechdive.com, accessed 2026-07-31) [web]. That attribution and vector are reported rather than established; Stryker has published no device count and secondary counts range from about 80,000 to 200,000 devices and 50GB to 50TB exfiltrated, so all counts are unverified. Because the attack was destructive rather than extortive there is no negotiated restore, only rebuild, and the vector was identity and device management rather than a product vulnerability, so the same class of exposure persists. Exposure: Q1 2026 organic growth 2.4%, adjusted operating margin down 180bps to 21.1%, adjusted EPS $2.60 and down 8.5%, the first adjusted EPS decline in the transcript record. Structural optimization and other special charges rose to $95m in Q2 2026 from $11m, and to $213m for six months from $52m. The only revenue figure in circulation is an analyst's roughly $375m estimate, which management neither confirmed nor decomposed. Leading indicators: further Item 1.05 filings; whether the special-charges line normalises; the FY2026 10-K's Item 1C, which can no longer use the FY2025 formulation that "cybersecurity risks have not materially affected us"; and any exfiltration-related claim. That FY2025 statement was filed 28 days before the incident, in an Item 1C describing annual third-party assessments, penetration tests, SOC 2 and ISO audits and quarterly leadership committees — none of which is described as covering privileged-access control in the device-management platform.

2. Second-half 2026 execution concentration — high, and dated. The FY2026 guide requires roughly 11% organic growth in H2 against 5.8% in H1, and roughly 14% adjusted EPS growth in H2 against 5.4% in H1, delivered by physical production of capital equipment rather than by demand. The quality of the Q2 beat is mixed: the CFO said it was "driven partially by the tariff refunds". Management declined to quantify three things on the Q2 call — the split of revenue between underlying demand and cyber catch-up, the size of the backlog, and the nature of the Inari supply failure. Six of eleven questioners pressed the back half. Leading indicators: Q3 2026 MedSurg US organic growth, specifically Medical and Endoscopy where the make-to-order deferral sits; Mako installation counts; whether the "elevated backlog" phrase survives a decelerating quarter; and hospital capital commentary from provider filings.

3. Peripheral Vascular goodwill of $3,203m at 12% headroom, in a business that just inflected negative — high. The annual test at 31 October 2025 was quantitative for this reporting unit and qualitative for every other, and found fair value exceeding carrying amount by 12%. Nine months later US Vascular organic sales declined 6.7% on a single-plant supply failure, Stryker ran an allocation process, kept its largest accounts and "let some of that business go", with back orders reaching "a manageable level" only by the end of Q3. The named discounted-cash-flow inputs are revenue growth, operating margin and the discount rate, and the supply failure moves all three the wrong way. The precedent is Spine: 10% headroom at the October 2023 test, $456m of impairment fourteen months later. For scale, group goodwill of $19,291m plus other intangibles of $5,681m exceeds shareholders' equity of $22,420m. Leading indicators: the 31 October 2026 test disclosed in the FY2026 10-K, specifically whether the unit is tested quantitatively again and what the headroom becomes; Vascular US organic growth returning to double digits; back-order clearance by end-Q3; and the PEERLESS II readout.

4. Serial-acquisition integration failure as a repeating mechanism — high. The FY2025 10-K added "a slower pace of integration than initially projected" to the acquisition risk factor and named Inari for the first time. Management confirms the mechanism is recurrent: on the Inari plant failure, "when we do acquisitions, we felt this pain before ... We did this with Sage. It's happened to us with Mako", and separately "We've gone through a lot of turmoil with the signing of noncompetes and a lot of sales force turnover." The realised precedent is spine. Exposure: FY2025 acquisition spend of $4,960m, total debt of $15,859m against $13,597m a year earlier, interest expense up 48% to $607m, and $732m of annual intangible amortization with $699m, $711m and $631m scheduled for 2026-2028, permanently excluded from adjusted EPS. Leading indicators: deal cadence against the resumed buyback; the acquisition-and-integration charge line; any further reporting-unit quantitative test; and Vascular and Smart Care organic growth as the integration report cards.

5. The German tax assessment of $765m against $403m of total unrecognized tax benefits — high. Stryker received a final audit report and assessments from the German Federal Central Tax Office for 2010-2017 of $754m and expects a further $11m. EY made it a critical audit matter. Stryker intends to defend through appeals "and, if necessary, litigation" and would seek offsetting foreign tax credits, which "may not be available on a timely basis or at all". The assessed amount is 23.6% of FY2025 net earnings and roughly $1.98 per diluted share [estimate: $765m over 386.4m shares]; total company-wide unrecognized tax benefits are $403m plus $96m of accrued interest, and Stryker states its reserve for this matter is unchanged from 2024. The structural driver is not a one-off: Stryker books $3,080m of pre-tax earnings internationally against $1,434m in the United States while the United States accounts for 75.7% of sales, and $11.7bn of foreign earnings are treated as indefinitely reinvested with the deferred tax "not practicable" to determine. Leading indicators: the unrecognized-tax-position balance, which grew from $349m to $403m in 2025; appeal milestones; domestic legislation of the January 2026 OECD safe harbours in each Pillar Two country; and cash taxes paid.

6. Tariffs — a $400m annual swing management has explicitly not offset — high. The sequence: about $200m estimated for 2025 (Q1 2025 call), reaffirmed at $200m (Q3 2025), then "approximately $400 million" for FY2026 including $200m incremental and first-half weighted (Q4 2025), then a Supreme Court ruling striking down certain tariffs with refunds whose "availability, timing, and amount ... remain uncertain" and the administration invoking alternative authorities including Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, then a $158m credit in Q2 2026 for "Reversal of 2025 tariffs". At $400m the exposure is 6.1% of FY2025 adjusted operating income and roughly $0.87 of adjusted EPS after tax [estimate: $400m over 386.4m shares at the guided 15.5% rate], 5.8% of the guidance midpoint. The reversal is not a resolution: the $158m is a reconciling item excluded from adjusted operating income, the refund is contingent, and replacement tariffs are already announced. No revised FY2026 tariff figure was given on 2026-07-30, so the largest controllable cost variable in the bridge is held at a stale number.

7. Price at zero while reimbursement pressure builds — medium-high. Price contribution went +0.4% (FY2025), +0.3% (Q1 2026), 0.0% (Q2 2026), and the six-month 2026 gross-margin bridge attributes 10bps to sales pricing. The FY2025 risk factors added "pressures on healthcare budgets" as a new named driver and upgraded cost-containment initiatives from "ongoing" to "ongoing and gaining increased attention". The specific live threat is the CY2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule proposal of cuts as much as 20%-plus on knees, hips and shoulders; management deflected with "the proposed rules are always so there sticker shock ... it ends up getting to a reasonable place", named no mitigation and pivoted to the site-of-care shift. Other named channels: China volume-based procurement, in Item 1A every year since FY2020 and sized nowhere; EU medical-device regulation phasing in through December 2028 with compliance costs booked as a recurring adjustment; healthcare-provider consolidation producing "larger enterprises with more bargaining power"; and Stryker's own admission that "We have also reduced prices for certain products due to increased competition."

8. The undisclosed capital order book — medium-high, a disclosure risk rather than an exposure. The backlog is the single input the FY2026 guide most depends on and is disclosed only as an adjective. Capital equipment and the order book is the most persistent recurring analyst question in the transcript record, present in every one of the last 18 quarters, and has never been sized. An investor cannot distinguish an elevated backlog caused by demand from one caused by Stryker's own production shortfall, which is precisely the ambiguity a three-week manufacturing outage creates. STERIS, by contrast, discloses backlog: $392.1m in Healthcare at 31 March 2026.

9. Manufacturing and single-source concentration — medium. "The manufacturing of certain of our product lines is concentrated in one or more plants or geographic regions" across 55 sites, with sole-source raw materials, components, finished devices and sterilization services where FDA rules require validation before use, making substitution slow. The operations head told the 2025 Investor Day "we tend to have a lot of small suppliers single sourced." Realised instances: the Inari single-plant failure; the standing FY2023-onward admission of lost sales; the Pangea launch constrained by kit complexity; and Triathlon Gold "just a little bit slower out of the gates than we would like, just because we lost production for a few weeks."

10. Product liability and the EU litigation regime change — medium. Rejuvenate and ABG II hip stems have been named in every 10-K since FY2016, LFIT V40 femoral heads since FY2018 and Wright legacy hip products since 2020. Recall-related charges are rising: $18m (2023), $40m (2024), $58m (2025). The FY2025 10-K sharpened the revised European Product Liability Directive's national adoption deadline to 9 December 2026 and retains the Collective Redress Directive, which "mandates a class action regime in each EU member state ... including product liability claims with medical devices". The product-liability accrual is $144m; Stryker is self-insured through a wholly-owned captive and warns coverage limits "may not be sufficient", and states the ultimate cost "could be materially different than the amount of the current estimates".

11. The decade-long ERP implementation — medium. "We are in the process of implementing a new commercial ERP system" has appeared in Item 1A in all ten years FY2016-FY2025. Stryker names the failure modes itself: inability "to process orders, ship products, provide services and customer support, send invoices and track payments, fulfill contractual obligations", which are the same functions the March 2026 incident disabled. A cutover problem during the H2 2026 backlog conversion would hit the same point twice. Leading indicator: any go-live disclosure in the MD&A or a change in the internal-control language.

12. Disclosure quality and the GAAP-to-adjusted wedge — medium. FY2025 GAAP diluted EPS of $8.40 against adjusted of $13.63 is a 62% gap, bridged by $732m of amortization, $660m of tax matters, $335m of acquisition and integration, $191m of structural optimization, $173m of inventory step-up, $170m of impairments, $58m of recall, $38m of medical device regulation and $17m of legal. Total segment operating income of $7,492m against GAAP operating income of $4,889m is a $2,603m wedge, $889m of it unallocated corporate cost. All guidance is non-GAAP only. Absent disclosures: no customer concentration, no GPO, no backlog, no country-level revenue, no units, ASPs or procedure counts, and from Q1 2026 no segment assets.

Which risks arrive together. Three of the live risks are dated to the same window and share one choke point: manufacturing and order fulfilment. A second IT event or an ERP cutover problem lands directly on the make-to-order capital backlog the FY2026 guide depends on, using the same systems that were wiped in March. Section 122 tariffs restoring the $400m cost while the $158m reversal is clawed back would hit gross margin at the same time as the cyber-remediation spend already guided to, against a 150bps three-year margin commitment. A slower Inari recovery both costs revenue and pressures the $3,203m of goodwill at 12% headroom, because the supply failure moves all three named discounted-cash-flow inputs adversely. If Stryker responds by deploying the M&A capacity it advertises, it adds integration risk on top. Price at zero removes the only lever available against tariff and reimbursement pressure simultaneously. Tax is the one large uncorrelated exposure: the German assessment and Pillar Two run on their own clock and would not be cushioned by a good operating quarter.

19. Source disclosure

Sources. Thirteen Stryker 10-Ks (FY2013-FY2025), eight 10-Qs (2024-Q1 through 2026-Q2), 49 earnings-call transcripts (Q2 2014 through Q2 2026), 62 presentation transcripts including three Investor Days and two deal calls, and twelve investor decks with 479 rendered slides. Peer filings for ZBH, JNJ, SNN, PEN, MDT, CNMD, BAX, STE, HCA, THC, SGRY, GMED, ENOV, ISRG, CRS, ITGR and SHC. SEC XBRL company facts for Stryker and eleven peers. Proxy statements 2018-2026. Bloomberg supplied prices, multiples, consensus estimates, broker recommendations, peer fundamentals for a 32-company reference class, and the public comparable table, all pulled 2026-07-31.

Data bootstrapped during the run. Five additional Stryker 10-Ks (FY2013-FY2015); ENOV filings (three) and five additional ZBH filings extending the series to FY2020; SHC, ITGR and CRS filings as value-chain layer proxies; the February 2025 credit agreement, pulled from EDGAR and recorded to the archive; and Inari Medical's FY2023 10-K, its last full-year public disclosure since the tender closed before the FY2024 filing deadline.

Gaps and failures. The sell-side digest holds zero coverage of Stryker — 40 reports, no mention of SYK or Stryker — so no research note, estimate-change detail or analyst rationale was available anywhere, and every statement about consensus rests on Bloomberg estimate data, management's narrative and analyst questions on the calls. The 10-K redline store does not cover Stryker, so the ten-year Item 1A diff was rebuilt by hand from the archived filings and no comparable diff of Item 1 or Item 7 exists. Bloomberg publishes no segment or business-line estimates for Stryker: BEST_SALES_SEGMENT, SALES_REV_TURN_SEGMENT and BEST_SEGMENT_ESTIMATES all return null or empty, so there is no external driver-level consensus to compare with the internal view. Bloomberg's guidance-history and estimate-revision-breadth fields are also null. The Call-extraction store has no results or comparison artifacts for Stryker and its guidance extraction stops at Q4 2025, so the twelve-year guidance scorecard was rebuilt by hand from 8-K exhibits. Form 4 and Form 144 filings were not available locally, so the eight-year decline in the founding family's holding is traced only through annual beneficial-ownership tables. Smith+Nephew publishes no segment gross margin, R&D or capex and no quarterly income statement; J&J publishes no franchise-level P&L for Orthopaedics; Karl Storz, Arthrex, Medline, Ferno-Washington, Zoll and Terumo Neuro publish no comparable financials at the business-line level. Zimmer Biomet had not reported a June-2026 quarter as of the run date. The 2025 Investor Day market-outlook data book, which is the entire basis for the served-market growth rate and the outgrowth claim, was not obtainable. National joint-registry robot-procedure tables were not retrievable.

Discrepancy log, summarised. Twelve differences were found between the printed 10-K statements, SEC XBRL, Bloomberg and a fourth vendor, and resolved in favour of the printed statement and the most recent restated basis. The material ones: XBRL is internally inconsistent for FY2016, mixing restated cost of sales with original gross profit, so no 2015-2016 margin series should be built from it; the FY2024 10-K eliminated the recall-charges income-statement line and restated SG&A for 2020-2023 without changing gross profit, operating income or net earnings; before FY2023 Stryker did not print a separate interest-expense line, so 2013-2022 interest coverage uses debt-note amounts and is approximate; the Note 14 total depreciation and amortization exceeds the sum of cash-flow depreciation and intangible amortization by $377m in 2025 and 20-25% for at least seven years, with no reconciliation in the filing, so two EBITDA answers exist; Bloomberg's net debt adds capitalized operating leases; Bloomberg's weighted-average share field is the basic count, not diluted; and Bloomberg's leverage ratios for Stryker are internally inconsistent with its own EBITDA field. Three segment recasts in twelve years sever the segment series at FY2021, FY2025 and Q1 2026.

Internal conflicts this document does not settle. Two consistency passes over the finished text corrected figures against the document's own tables and left the following unresolved. A reader who meets them should know which value the rest of the document uses.

  • Enterprise value. The header computes $136,016m from the filings and reports Bloomberg's $135,266m, explaining the difference as Bloomberg including $501m of capitalised operating leases. Capitalising leases raises enterprise value, so that explanation cannot produce a Bloomberg figure $750m lower. The header multiples use the filing-derived $136,016m; the Section 16 comparable table uses Bloomberg's $135,266m for every company including Stryker. The same as-of difference runs through the price: Section 16 carries Stryker at the $324.71 intraday quote the header uses, while every body table uses the $323.49 daily-history close for the same date, as the header note explains.
  • Consolidated ROIC for 2025 on a normalised 21% tax. Section 7's point 7 previously gave 11.1% against 11.9% in Section 3.2 and the Section 3.3 peer table; it has been set to 11.9%, the figure the rest of the document uses and the one the peer table computes on a consistent basis across fourteen companies. The denominator behind the two figures is still not settled and neither is exactly reproducible. Section 10.1's year-end invested capital of $34,268m against FY2025 GAAP operating income of $4,889m taxed at 21% gives 11.3%; Section 13.1's normalised-15%-tax series of 13.0% converts to 12.1% at 21% — that series appears to run on average rather than year-end invested capital, because 2016's printed 17.2% reproduces on the average of the $8,519m and $12,848m endpoints but not on the year-end figure. Section 7's 2020 point of 7.2% sits below the 8.1% that Section 13.1's 8.7% converts to, so that whole series is on the tighter denominator. A human should fix the invested-capital convention and restate the ROIC series once on it.
  • J&J MedTech hips growth in Q2 2026 appears three times on three apparent bases: +4.9% (Sections 3.1 and 3.3), +4.0% operational (Section 4.1) and +3.5% (Section 6.1, in a US comparison). Only the +4.0% figure names its basis.
  • Penumbra's status. Section 3.2 records Boston Scientific's agreement of 2026-01-15 to acquire Penumbra at an enterprise value of about $14.5bn ($374 a share), while Section 16 carries Penumbra as a standalone at $319.95 with $12,157m of enterprise value and independent consensus estimates through FY2029, and Sections 4.2 and 7 treat it as an ongoing independent competitor. Whether the transaction is still live was not established.
  • Days inventory outstanding. Two values are in the document and neither is verified here. The computed decade range is 194-241 days, which Section 10 now carries; Sections 1.2 and 17.2 state the metric never dropped below 197. An earlier pass overwrote the computed 194 to 197 to match the assertion, which resolved nothing, and the overwrite has been reversed. A human must recompute days inventory outstanding from the ten-year inventory and cost-of-sales series and then correct either the 194 low or the two "never below 197" statements. Nothing else in the document turns on which is right.
  • The Q2 2026 tariff reversal. The $158m credit was described in three places as worth 260bps of gross margin; $158m on the quarter's $6,589m of net sales is 240bps, and 240bps is now used throughout. The 260bps figure is consistent with a year-over-year bridge line rather than a single-quarter ratio, and the same caution applies to the 110bps of lower inventory step-up amortization quoted beside it, which is a year-over-year movement and not a second deduction from the 68.3% reported level.
  • "The smallest of the five revenue drivers." Sections 7 and 17.3 describe Knees and Hips this way, while the Section 17.3 sensitivity table contains four revenue-growth rows (one of which bundles three MedSurg lines). The count could not be reconciled to the table.
  • Section 15.1's 2026 year-to-date multiples are Bloomberg fields that do not reproduce from the document's own inputs: the 20x consensus forward P/E against $323.49 over FY2027E adjusted EPS of $16.75 gives 19.3x, and the 5.2x price-to-book against $124,550m of market capitalisation over $22,420m of equity gives 5.6x. Sections 15.5 and 16 use the internally computed figures.
  • FY2025 net leverage is 1.9x in Section 12 and 1.8x in Section 13.1. Both are correct on their own EBITDA basis, and the $377m gap between the Note 14 and cash-flow measures is described above; neither section states which basis it uses.
  • The 2016 adjusted operating margin is 25.5% in Sections 10 and 13.1 and 25.6% on the 2023 Investor Day slide reproduced in Appendix A. The Appendix A commentary has been aligned to the Section 13.1 basis; the slide caption keeps the deck's own figure.
  • Emerging-market growth on the 2021 analyst-day slide. The Appendix A bullet gives 15-20% constant currency and the caption on the same slide gives 18-20%, from the same source. The deck was not re-read to settle it, and nothing else in the document turns on the difference.
  • Two figures on the 2021 analyst-day scorecard slides do not reconcile to Section 13.1. The caption reads 131bps of cumulative operating-margin expansion over 2016-2019, against Section 13.1's 25.5% (2016) to 26.3% (2019), which is 80bps, and the 2023 deck's own 25.6% start, which is 70bps. The companion caption reads free cash flow averaging $1.7bn at 66% conversion over 2016-2019, against Section 13.1's free-cash-flow row of $1,322m, $961m, $2,038m and $1,542m, an average of $1,466m, and Section 10.1's conversion of 65.0%, 39.0%, 73.3% and 49.1%, an average of 56.6%. Both captions are reported as the deck prints them. A human must establish whether the deck uses a different margin and free-cash-flow definition before either figure is quoted as Stryker's record.
  • The FY2016 GAAP tax rate used in the incremental-return calculation. Section 10.1 taxes FY2016 GAAP operating income at 14.3% to reach NOPAT of $1,864m and a 7.7% incremental GAAP return, but 14.3% is the rate the front matter attributes to FY2024. FY2016's GAAP effective rate appears nowhere in this document, so the 7.7% cannot be checked here and should be re-derived from the FY2016 10-K.
  • The $6bn US venous-thromboembolism figure. The January 2025 Inari deal deck caption previously called $6bn "the US mechanical-thrombectomy segment" while the November 2025 Investor Day slide sizes the same $6bn-plus as the whole VTE pool of which mechanical thrombectomy is 14-19%. The Inari caption has been aligned to Section 4.3's component decomposition — $2.6bn pulmonary embolism, $3.0bn deep-vein thrombosis and $1bn chronic venous disease — which is the reading Sections 6.1, 17.2 and Appendix C all use. The January 2025 deck's own label was not re-read.

Web sources. Roughly 45 external pages are cited from about 30 domains, concentrated in: company investor-relations and press releases (stryker, jnj, bostonscientific, olympus-global, ftc.gov, cms.gov — 12); trade press (medtechdive, massdevice, orthospinenews, beckersspine, medcitynews — 10); peer-reviewed and clinical literature (boneandjoint.org.uk, pubmed, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, ajmc, jorthobusiness, arthroplastyjournal, bmjgroup — 9); industry and market data (kaufmanhall, ascdata via Becker's, constructconnect, datalilyai, gminsights, researchandmarkets — 8); and market aggregators (financialcontent, stockanalysis, investing.com, cbonds — 6). Every one cited for a material claim is quoted verbatim in Appendix B.

Claims flagged as [web, unverified]. Four. The third-party robot installed-base estimates in Section 2 (ROSA at 1,300-plus systems and CORI at 1,100-plus globally at YE2025) come from market-research summaries that could not be re-verified; Stryker's own "more than 3,000" and Smith+Nephew's "over 1,100" are the reliable figures. The Kaufman Hall regional operating-margin percentages for year-to-date May 2026 rest on a Flash Report summary rather than the underlying monthly document. The Medicare-certified ambulatory-surgery-centre counts in Section 1.5 (6,504 at Q2 2025 and 6,566 at Q4 2025, from ASC Data via Becker's ASC Review) have no retrievable permalink. And the secondary device and exfiltration counts for the March 2026 cyber incident (80,000-200,000 devices, 50GB-50TB) are attacker or researcher claims that Stryker has never confirmed, and are reported as unverified in Section 18 rather than used.

Estimates by method. Thirty triangulated figures are tagged [estimate: method] in the body, all with bounds. By method: residual or back-out from a disclosed aggregate, 10 (the capital-core gross margin, the transferred-bundle economics, legacy Vascular organic growth, core Endoscopy visualization, ex-US construct price, implant unit cost, the LIFEPAK input cost, restated FY2025 MedSurg revenue, the Zimmer Biomet trauma comparable, Q1 2026 line and segment figures); triangulation from two or more disclosed ratios, 8 (knee and hip procedure counts, the Inari per-procedure price, Mako revenue per system, Mako net adds, Orthopaedic Instruments annualised revenue, the Mako facility cost build, the Inari supply drag, the model's net segment transfer); arithmetic recomputation of disclosed figures, 7 (incremental adjusted and GAAP ROIC, the 2018 tax benefit per share, the performance-stock-unit metric ex-tax, the German assessment per share, the tariff EPS effect, consensus implied organic growth, the required H2 organic rate); and counterfactual or scenario arithmetic, 5 (the price-erosion-arrest value, the served-market mix arithmetic, the 2020 buyback forgone value, the refinancing cost, the M&A capacity revenue equivalent).

Two claims that an earlier draft got wrong, and the basis of the rest. Corrected in the body: the assertion that Stryker has never disclosed any deal-level return standard (it disclosed two, on Wright and Inari, and reported against neither), and the assertion that the Investor Day venous-thromboembolism slide is internally inconsistent (it is not; the arithmetic reconciles once the donut-hole totals are read correctly). Basis notes on figures a reader could otherwise misread: the shoulder-share donor attribution is an inference rather than a disclosure; management asserts continuity rather than a step-down in its 200-300bps outgrowth assumption; the 150bps margin commitment is an acceleration of the previously stated 30bps-a-year floor as well as a reduction against the 105bps a year just delivered; the Q1 2026 recast moved the power-tool franchise out of MedSurg, not Mako; the robotic-knee episode-cost figures are $28,204 against $32,253, not the lower pair originally cited; the adjusted-versus-GAAP incremental-ROIC gap is partly a tax-rate difference; the $362m spine valuation allowance falls in 2024, not 2025; and Penumbra's 15.6% Q1 2026 figure is total company revenue growth, not US venous thromboembolism.

Assumption review. Twenty-nine model assumptions were tested and are listed in Section 17.2. Ten hold, seventeen are weak and two are refuted. Every weak and refuted assumption is flagged in Section 17.2 beside the driver it affects, with the counter-argument stated.

External datasets. None were pulled. The two identified for this company are described in Appendix C with the reasons one of them is the wrong endpoint for a device manufacturer.

20. What we still don't know, and the monitoring list

Ten gaps are material enough to change a conclusion.

  • No dollar capital order book, backlog, remaining performance obligation or book-to-bill exists in any filing. This is the single largest unquantifiable in the document. It is the stated support for a second half that has to grow roughly 11% organically, and it makes Section 17's FY2026 base case and Section 14's internal-versus-external comparison unverifiable in their most consequential year. The only balance-sheet handle, contract liabilities, declined $27m in H1 2026. One untried proxy remains: if make-to-order capital shipments were deferred rather than lost, finished goods and work in progress should have built through H1 2026 against $5,310m of inventory at YE2025.
  • International is 24.3% of revenue and its growth gap is unexplained. The 580bp gap between US growth of 12.2% and international growth of 6.4% constant currency in FY2025 is unexplained; China volume-based procurement and post-MDR Europe are named as headwinds and sized nowhere, while Smith+Nephew and Olympus both quantify the same China effect in their own filings. The forward model runs eight years on consolidated line growth with no regional split, so the fade could be materially faster than the 6.9% base-case revenue CAGR.
  • The Medical line is three businesses with three cycles reported as one $4,204m number. Emergency-care municipal budgets, acute-care capital, Sage disposables and Smart Care software have different exposures and different durations, and the model's second-largest fade assumption rests on the undecomposed line.
  • Neuro Cranial is $2,485m growing 16.3% and is analysed far less than Vascular, which is smaller and slower. The interventional-spine growth driver is unsized, the split between organic growth and the Vertos, NICO and Cerus acquisitions is untested, and no competitor share exists for the line.
  • The recurring-versus-capital mix has two incompatible answers. At most 10% of group revenue is contractually recurring on the services-over-time disclosure, while management's only durability quantification is roughly 25% capital and 75% procedurally driven. Those two figures measure different things and should not be reconciled by choosing one.
  • The ASC channel is both a volume tailwind and a pricing threat, and the deciding fact is not disclosed. ASC device spend is 26.6% of USPI revenue and rising against 15.0% at hospitals, and a full Mako plus implant consumes 77% of the Medicare ambulatory knee payment. Nobody discloses the price or gross-margin differential between an ASC placement and a hospital placement.
  • Sports medicine is the one sub-market where Stryker is clearly sub-scale — third at 13% of a $7.0bn market behind Arthrex at 35% and Smith+Nephew at 25% — and no work here tests what a distant-third position does to Endoscopy's returns, or whether a private competitor Stryker cannot buy is a structural disadvantage.
  • Restated segment operating income on the current basis exists for only two quarters. The forward model, the moat's margin tests and Section 13's segment table are all built on a basis Stryker will never report again. Two sources could close it: Stryker's own restated 2023-2025 quarterly revenue posted to its investor site, and extending the recast bridge computed for H1 2025 back through FY2023.
  • The peer share series is two years long, and those are the two years in which two of the three competitors were disrupting themselves. The comparison rests on FY2025 filings alone for Zimmer Biomet, J&J and Smith+Nephew. J&J was suppressing reported revenue with a restructuring programme whose charge went from $307m to $17m, and Zimmer Biomet was rebuilding its US sales force. The 191bps share gain cannot be separated from competitor self-disruption on a two-year window.
  • No downside scenario is calibrated on the one downturn in the record. Orthopaedics posted a 123% decremental margin in 2020 and MedSurg a negative 6.5% incremental margin in 2022; US hospital operating margins were down 5% year over year through May 2026 and HCA's Q2 2026 surgeries declined 4.4% outpatient and 2.3% inpatient. The model's bear case is a slow H2 2026 conversion, not a joint elective-plus-capital downturn.

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights and key slides

Twelve decks and 479 rendered slides sit in the archive, spanning 2015 to 2025. Three of the four annual-meeting decks have no extractable text layer and two are unusable screen captures. The decks add material the filings do not contain, and in three places they contradict the filings' own framing. The additive insights appear in the body sections named below; this is the consolidated view.

  • Competitor-by-competitor market share exists in exactly one Stryker document, and it prices the Wright Medical deal. The FY2025 10-K discloses no market share anywhere. The November 2018 analyst meeting prints 2017 US share for two markets, and the matching call transcript does not speak the numbers; the presenters point at the slide. US Foot and Ankle: Stryker 22%, Wright Medical 22%, Synthes 14%, Arthrex 9%, Smith & Nephew 7%, Zimmer 6%, Integra 5% [deck: Analyst Meeting 2018-11-08, slide 32]. US Shoulder: Zimmer 32%, Wright 22%, Synthes 17%, DJO 10%, Exactech 7%, Stryker 6% [slide 33]. On those shares Stryker plus Wright is 44% of foot and ankle, a clear first at roughly three times the next competitor, and 28% of shoulder, second behind Zimmer, from sixth. The 2023 deck then claims that outcome. Wright bought a position, not a technology. Informs §4 and §11.
  • The only public decomposition of the addressable market below the segment is four years old and shows Stryker exiting its largest block. The 2021 analyst day sizes Orthopaedics and Spine at $36bn and MedSurg and Neurotechnology at $36bn, business unit by business unit [slides 39 and 53]. Spine was the largest single block at $13bn growing 3%, and Stryker exited US spinal implants four years later. The pools growing double digit were Surgical Technologies, Sage and Neurovascular — and the three acquisitions Stryker made after that deck (Vocera 2022, care.ai 2024, Inari 2025) all sit in or adjacent to them rather than in the $27bn of low-single-digit joint replacement and spine. Informs §4 and §11.
  • The operating-margin goalposts have moved four times and are only visible in sequence. 190-250bps over five years (2016) became 30-50bps a year (2018), then a minimum 30bps a year excluding large-deal dilution (2021), then about 200bps through 2025 plus 30-plus bps a year (2023), then 150-plus bps through 2028 inclusive of tuck-in dilution (2025) [decks 2016 slide 40, 2018 slides 54 and 61, 2021 slide 27, 2023 slides 53 and 55, 2025 slide 65]. Delivered: adjusted operating margin of 25.5% in 2016 and 26.3% in 2025 on the Section 13.1 basis, roughly 80bps in nine years against 190-250bps promised for the first five alone. The 2025 deck's margin chart anchors on 2019 and 2023, which removes 2016-2018 and the 2022 trough from the picture. Informs §8 and §10.
  • The outgrowth claim rests on a benchmark that moved between deck vintages. The same 2016-2019 period is 7.4% against 4.4% in the 2021 deck and 8% against 5% in the 2025 deck [2021 slide 22; 2025 slide 62]. Both report +300bps, and both the numerator and the denominator moved about 60bps. The peer set was footnoted as "Company research of 20 companies" in 2016 and 2018 and as "SYK competitor peer set" with no count and no names from 2021. Informs §6 and §8.
  • The buyback footnote is a flat statement of intent that appears in no filing. "No buybacks have been executed since 2019 and there are no plans to resume activity" [2025 slide 64], alongside dividend growth at "a modest pace". Eight months later the policy reversed. Informs §10.
  • The ASC channel is quantified in exactly one place. 460-plus partnerships as of September 2025, roughly 60% expansions or renovations and 40% new builds, 200-plus Mako systems contracted for ASCs, 360-plus deals with tailored financial solutions, 15 dedicated regional managers, and an average of seven business units per deal [2025 slide 21]. The seven-business-unit figure is the only cross-sell metric Stryker publishes anywhere, and the financing line is the only public indication that Stryker extends customer financing at scale. Informs §1 and §5.
  • Two platform cadences are documented in the decks and nowhere in the filings. The endoscopy camera platform ran 1188 (2004), 1288 (2006), 1488 (2008), 1088 (2012), 1588 (2015), 1688 (2019), 1788 (2023) — a new capital platform every three to four years, each a fresh replacement cycle [2023 slide 24]. Power instruments ran OP90 (1983), Turbo helmet (1993), System 9 (2023), Steri-Shield 8 (2025) [2025 slide 26]. The camera cadence is the mechanism behind the Endoscopy revenue series and directly contradicts the forward model's assumption that the line fades because no successor has been dated. Informs §2 and §17.
  • The longest continuous single-business revenue series Stryker has published is in a 2018 deck. Global Endoscopy sales run from roughly $205m in 1999 to roughly $1,650m in 2017, an 11-12% CAGR over eighteen years with a single down year in 2009 [2018 slide 37]. It is not reconstructable from the 10-Ks. Informs §1.
  • Vocera's renewal rate is the only recurring-software retention figure ever published. A $1bn addressable market and "nearly 100% software renewal rate" [2023 slide 44]. No renewal rate, annual recurring revenue, remaining performance obligation or software-revenue split appears in any 10-K or 10-Q. Informs §3.
  • Inari's deceleration is printed on the slide Stryker used to justify the price. Revenue of $51m (2019) rising to $603m (2024E) with year-over-year growth of +38%, +29% and +22% for 2022, 2023 and 2024E [M&A deck 2025-01-06, slide 7], against $4.9bn of equity value — roughly 8.1x forward revenue for an asset whose growth had halved across three consecutive years. Management neither addressed the deceleration nor sized the contribution required to justify the price. Informs §11.
  • International is shrinking as a share of the business while being sold as the opportunity. US 68% of 2014 sales, 73% of 2019 and 74% of 2022 [2015 slide 21; 2021 slide 18; 2023 slide 10], while constant-currency growth in Europe ran 9-10% and emerging markets 15-20%. The mix shift is a statement about how much faster the US business grew and about US-weighted acquisitions. The 2025 deck drops the international slide entirely. Informs §6 and §13.
  • The 2025 business-unit map is a leading indicator of the Q1 2026 reportable-line recast. Spine has disappeared as a division, interventional spine sits inside Neuro Cranial, Vascular is a named business containing Inari and Neurovascular, Smart Care is a named business inside Medical, and Mako and enabling technologies sit under Joint Replacement [2025 slides 11 and 19]. The deck showed the structure before the filings reported it. Informs §1.
  • A business that once had a customer panel and 270 customers has vanished without explanation. Stryker Performance Solutions had two slides and a customer panel at the 2016 analyst meeting — more than 270 customers, more than 700,000 episodes, $110m of customer savings in 2015, 78% discharge-to-home against a 51% Medicare average — framed as the answer to CMS's episode-payment agenda [2016 slides 18, 33-36]. It appears in no deck after 2016 and in no business-unit map. Nothing in the archive explains it. Informs §9.
  • What the decks never disclose. No deck shows segment operating margin, price and volume decomposition, average selling prices, the capital order book, Mako system pricing or lease economics, robot revenue, software or service revenue, customer concentration, or a country-level revenue split. Every financial slide is consolidated and non-GAAP.

Attribution and vector are reported rather than established, and no device count is company-confirmed.

Appendix C — External data sources

Two external datasets were identified for this company from the registry. Neither was pulled; the deep dive does not auto-fetch them, and this is a menu rather than data. Each entry states what it is, what it measures and what it would settle here.

clinicaltrials.gov trial starts — free API at https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies, measuring trial starts by phase and sponsor over time. Stryker sponsors device studies across its portfolio: Mako outcomes registries, the Inari venous-thromboembolism programme including PEERLESS and DEFIANCE, and Tornier shoulder studies. Sponsor-level trial-start counts for Stryker against Zimmer Biomet, Smith+Nephew, Medtronic, Penumbra and Globus Medical are the only measurable proxy for relative clinical-evidence investment, which is the currency of surgeon adoption in orthopaedics. That is precisely the ground on which Section 2 finds Mako weakest — RASKAL showed no superiority at two years — and on which the whole Vascular base case rests, because expanding mechanical thrombectomy from 14-19% penetration requires randomised evidence against anticoagulation rather than share taken from a competing device. It would strengthen §2, §4 and §6, and it would give the forward model's Vascular assumption an external anchor it currently lacks. One caveat: device trials are far less standardised than drug phases, so phase fields will be sparse. Not yet pulled (available on demand).

openFDA drug approvals — free API at https://api.fda.gov/drug/drugsfda.json, measuring drug application approvals and submissions by sponsor over time. This is the wrong endpoint for this company and should not be presented as coverage of it. Stryker is a medical device manufacturer with no drug applications, so a sponsor query against the drug endpoint returns essentially nothing. The device-side equivalents that would inform this analysis are absent from the registry as configured, and their absence is itself a finding worth stating: openFDA 510(k) clearances (device/510k.json) and PMA approvals (device/pma.json) would give a clearance-cadence series against competitors, testing the launch-cadence claim in Section 2 directly; openFDA device recalls and enforcement (device/recall.json, device/enforcement.json) and MAUDE adverse-event reports (device/event.json) would supply the recall and adverse-event denominator that Section 18's product-liability entry has to describe qualitatively because Stryker discloses only the charge, never the event count; CMS Medicare procedure volumes for MS-DRG 469 and 470 would give the demand denominator for the roughly 40% of Orthopaedics revenue that is knees and hips, which currently rests on a single published abstract of unverified payer basis; and CMS Open Payments would be the only direct measure of surgeon-relationship spend, which is the mechanism every moat argument in Section 3 terminates in and which no filing sizes. Not yet pulled (available on demand), and the registered endpoint would need to be repointed at the device APIs before it returns anything useful for this company.
